## HISTORY AND DERIVATION OF PIPING FLEXIBILITY ANALYSIS

![Fig. A.11 The angle $\\psi$ for circular members counterclockwise.](figures/MWK_1956_p0318_fig01_fig-a-11-the-angle-psi-for-circular-memb.png)

![Fig. A.12 The angle $\\psi$ for circular members clockwise.](figures/MWK_1956_p0318_fig02_fig-a-12-the-angle-psi-for-circular-memb.png)

For a circular member the *direction* may be either counterclockwise, or clockwise as the member is viewed in its working plane. For the counterclockwise direction the angle $\psi$ in the integrals for the shape coefficients is replaced by $(\alpha + \phi)$ where $\alpha$ is a constant angle, positive if measured from the negative vertical axis in the counterclockwise direction. The angle $\phi$ is a variable, positive in the counterclockwise direction. See Fig. A.11.

For the clockwise direction the angle $\psi$ in integrals for the shape coefficients is replaced by

$(\alpha - \phi)$ where $\alpha$ is defined in the same way as for the counterclockwise direction, and $\phi$ is a variable angle positive in the clockwise direction (Fig. A.12).

It should be noted that in the integration of the shape coefficients for concentrated loading the *counterclockwise* direction is used. If the *clockwise* direction is used the numerical values for the shape coefficients will be the same although the formulas will differ.

![Fig. A.13 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for weight loading of circular members in the z-plane.](figures/MWK_1956_p0318_fig03_fig-a-13-counterclockwise-integration-of.png)

$$l = R\phi \quad dl = R \, d\phi$$
$$x = a + R \sin (\alpha + \phi)$$
$$y = b - R \cos (\alpha + \phi)$$

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\int_0^\phi x \, dl}{\int_0^\phi dl} = a + R \frac{\sin (\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha}{\phi}$$

Integrations of the shape coefficients for weight loading applied to circular members are as follows, beginning with a member in the z-plane taken in the *counterclockwise* direction, as shown in Fig. A.13:

$$w_a = \int_0^\phi kQR^4 [\cos \alpha - \cos (\alpha + \phi) - \phi \sin (\alpha + \phi)] \, d\phi = kQR^4 [\Phi(\cos (\alpha + \phi) + \cos \alpha] - 2[\sin (\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha]$$

$$w_{ab} = +bw_a + w'_{aa}$$

where $w'_{aa} = -\int_0^\phi kQR^5 [\cos \alpha - \cos (\alpha + \phi) - \phi \sin (\alpha + \phi)] \cos (\alpha + \phi) \, d\phi$

$$= +kQR^5 \left\{ \frac{\Phi}{2} \left[ 1 - \frac{\cos 2(\alpha + \phi)}{2} \right] + \tfrac{3}{8} [\sin 2(\alpha + \Phi) - \sin 2\alpha] - \cos \alpha [\sin (\alpha + \Phi) - \sin \alpha] \right\}$$

$$w_{aa} = -aw_a + w'_{aa}$$

where $w'_{aa} = \int_0^\phi kQR^5 [\cos \alpha - \cos (\alpha + \phi)] \sin (\alpha + \phi) \, d\phi$

$$= kQR^5 \left\{ \frac{\Phi}{4} [\Phi - \sin 2(\alpha + \Phi)] - \tfrac{3}{8} [\cos 2(\alpha + \Phi) - \cos 2\alpha] - \cos \alpha [\cos (\alpha + \Phi) - \cos \alpha] \right\}$$

---

![Fig. A.14 Clockwise integration of shape coefficients for weight of circular members in the x-plane.](figures/MWK_1956_p0319_fig01_clockwise-integration-of-shape-coefficie.png)

$$l = R\psi \qquad dl = R\,d\psi$$
$$x = a + R\sin(\alpha - \psi)$$
$$y = b - R\cos(\alpha - \psi)$$
$$\bar{x} = \frac{\int_0^\alpha x\,dl}{\int_0^\alpha dl} = a + R\,\frac{\cos(\alpha - \phi) - \cos\alpha}{\phi}$$

For $x$-plane members taken in the *clockwise* direction (Fig. A.14):

$$w_a = \int_0^\phi kQR^4[\cos(\alpha - \phi) - \cos\alpha + \phi\sin(\alpha - \phi)]\,d\phi$$
$$\quad = -kQR^4\{\phi[\cos(\alpha - \phi) + \cos\alpha] + 2[\sin(\alpha - \phi) - \sin\alpha]\}$$

$$w_{ab} = +bw_a + w'_{ab}$$

where: $w'_{ab} = -\int_0^\phi kQR^4[\cos(\alpha - \phi) - \cos\alpha + \phi\sin(\alpha - \phi)]\cos(\alpha - \phi)\,d\phi$

$$\quad = -kQR^4\left\{\frac{\phi}{2}\left[\Phi + \frac{1 - \cos 2(\alpha - \phi)}{2}\right] - \tfrac{1}{8}[\sin 2(\alpha - \phi) - \sin 2\alpha] + \cos\alpha[\sin(\alpha - \phi) - \sin\alpha]\right\}$$

$$w_{aa} = -aw_a + w'_{aa}$$

where: $w'_{aa} = -\int_0^\phi kQR^4[\cos(\alpha - \phi) - \cos\alpha + \phi\sin(\alpha - \phi)]\sin(\alpha - \phi)\,d\phi$

$$\quad = kQR^4\left\{\frac{\phi}{8}[\Phi + \sin 2(\alpha - \Phi)] - \tfrac{1}{8}[\cos 2(\alpha - \phi) - \cos 2\alpha] + \cos\alpha[\cos(\alpha - \phi) - \cos\alpha]\right\}$$

*Note:* The above expressions for $w_a$, $w_{ab}$, $w_{aa}$ in the clockwise direction may be obtained by substituting $-\phi$ for $+\phi$ in the corresponding expressions in the counterclockwise direction. This rule is valid for all shape coefficients for uniform loading. Hence, only the integration for the counterclockwise direction will be shown for $y$-plane and $z$-plane members.

---

HISTORY AND DERIVATION OF PIPING FLEXIBILITY ANALYSIS 319

![Fig. A.15 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for weight of circular members in the y-plane.](figures/MWK_1956_p0320_fig01_counterclockwise-integration-shape-coeff.png)

$$l = R\varphi \quad dl = R\, d\varphi$$
$$x = b - R\cos(\alpha + \varphi)$$
$$z = a + R\sin(\alpha + \varphi)$$

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\int_0^\varphi x\, dl}{\int_0^\varphi dl} = b + R\frac{\sin\alpha - \sin(\alpha + \varphi)}{\varphi}$$

$$\bar{z} = \frac{\int_0^\varphi z\, dl}{\int_0^\varphi dl} = a + R\frac{\cos\alpha - \cos(\alpha + \varphi)}{\varphi}$$

For y-plane members taken in the *counterclockwise* direction (Fig. A.15):

$$w_x = -\int_0^\varphi QR^3[\cos\alpha - \cos(\alpha + \phi)][k\cos^2(\alpha + \phi) + 1.3\sin^2(\alpha + \phi)]\, d\phi$$

$$\quad + \int_0^\varphi QR^3[\sin\alpha - \sin(\alpha + \phi) + \phi\cos(\alpha + \phi)](1.3 - k)\sin(\alpha + \phi)\cos(\alpha + \phi)\, d\phi$$

$$= -QR^3\left\{k\left[\frac{\Phi}{2}\cos\alpha - \cos(\alpha + \Phi) + 0.75\sin\alpha + 0.25\sin(\alpha + 2\Phi)\right]\right.$$

$$\quad \left. + 1.3\left[\frac{\Phi}{2}\cos\alpha + \Phi\cos(\alpha + \phi) - \sin(\alpha + \phi) + 1.25\sin\alpha - 0.25\sin(\alpha + 2\Phi)\right]\right\}$$

$$w_x = +\int_0^\varphi QR^3[\sin\alpha - \sin(\alpha + \phi) + \phi\cos(\alpha + \phi)][1.3\cos^2(\alpha + \phi) + k\sin^2(\alpha + \phi)]\, d\phi$$

$$\quad - \int_0^\varphi QR^3[\cos\alpha - \cos(\alpha + \phi) - \phi\sin(\alpha + \phi)](1.3 - k)\sin(\alpha + \phi)\cos(\alpha + \phi)\, d\phi$$

$$= QR^3\left\{k\left[\frac{\Phi}{2}\sin\alpha + \cos(\alpha + \phi) - 0.75\cos\alpha - 0.25\cos(\alpha + 2\Phi)\right] + 1.3\left[\frac{\Phi}{2}\sin\alpha\right.\right.$$

$$\quad \left.\left. + \Phi\sin(\alpha + \phi) + \cos(\alpha + \phi) - 1.25\cos\alpha + 0.25\cos(\alpha + 2\Phi)\right]\right\}$$

$$w_{xz} = +aw_x - bw_z + w'_{xz}$$

where: $w'_{xz} = -\int_0^\varphi QR^4 \sin(\alpha + \phi)\left\{k\left[\frac{\cos\alpha}{2} - \cos(\alpha + \phi) + \frac{\cos(\alpha + 2\phi)}{2}\right]\right.$

$$\quad \left. + 1.3\left[\frac{\cos\alpha}{2} - \phi\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \frac{\cos(\alpha + 2\phi)}{2}\right]\right\}d\phi$$

$$\quad + \int_0^\varphi QR^4 \cos(\alpha + \phi)\left\{k\left[\frac{\sin\alpha}{2} - \sin(\alpha + \phi) + \frac{\sin(\alpha + 2\phi)}{2}\right]\right.$$

$$\quad \left. + 1.3\left[\frac{\sin\alpha}{2} + \phi\cos(\alpha + \phi) - \frac{\sin(\alpha + 2\phi)}{2}\right]\right\}d\phi = 1.3QR^4\left[\frac{\Phi^2}{2} + \cos\Phi - 1\right]$$

---

![Fig. A.16 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for weight of circular members in the x-plane.](figures/MWK_1956_p0321_fig01_fig-a16-counterclockwise-integration-sha.png)

For x-plane members taken in the *counterclockwise* direction (Fig. A.16):

$$w_b = -\int_0^{\alpha+\Phi} kQR^4 [\sin\alpha + \phi) + \phi \cos(\alpha+\phi)] d\phi$$

$$= -kQR^4 \{\Phi[\sin(\alpha+\Phi) + \sin(\alpha+\Phi) - \cos\alpha)]\} + 2[\cos(\alpha+\Phi) - \cos\alpha]\}$$

$$w_{ba} = -qw_b + w'_{ba}$$

where $w'_{ba} = +\int_0^{\Phi} kQR^4 [\Phi[\sin\alpha - \sin(\alpha+\phi)] \sin(\alpha+\phi)] d\phi$

$$= -kQR^4 \left\{\frac{\Phi}{2}\left[1 + \frac{\cos 2(\alpha+\Phi)}{2}\right] - \frac{3}{8}[\sin 2(\alpha+\Phi) - \sin 2\alpha] + \sin\alpha[\cos(\alpha+\Phi) - \cos\alpha]\right\}$$

$$w_{bb} = +bw_b + w'_{bb}$$

where $w'_{bb} = +\int_0^{\Phi} kQR^4 [\sin\alpha - \sin(\alpha+\phi) + \phi \cos(\alpha+\phi)] \cos(\alpha+\phi) d\phi$

$$= +kQR^4 \left\{\frac{\Phi}{2}[\Phi + \sin 2(\alpha+\Phi)] + \frac{1}{4}[\cos 2(\alpha+\Phi) - \cos 2\alpha] + \sin\alpha[\sin(\alpha+\Phi) - \sin\alpha]\right\}$$

# HISTORY AND DERIVATION OF PIPING FLEXIBILITY ANALYSIS

As mentioned previously in connection with the formulas of Table A.4, the effective wind load on a member is taken as the unit wind load multiplied by the length of the member's projection on a plane perpendicular to the wind direction. If the working plane of the member is perpendicular to the wind, the wind load is simply $w l$. The shape coefficients are then the same as those already found for weight loading, identified as $w_b$, $w_a$, and $w_{ab}$. For members in planes parallel to the wind, the wind load is $w l'$ where $l'$ represents the projected length of the member on a plane perpendicular to the wind direction.

![Fig. A.17 Integration of shape coefficients for straight members in the p-plane acted upon by z-wind.](figures/MWK_1956_p0322_fig01_fig-a-17-integration-of-shape-coefficien.png)

Formulas for calculating shape coefficients $w_b$, $w_{bb}$, and $w_{ab}$ are now derived for a straight member in the z-plane, acted upon by a wind parallel to the z (horizontal) axis as shown in Fig. A.17.

The relationships for $l'$, $\bar{y}'$, and $z$ accompanying Fig. A.17 are readily derived therefrom. The two functions expressing $l'$ are necessary since the unit load is considered positive and thus the total load $wl'$ and the length $l'$ itself must remain positive for any value of $\alpha$.

Performing the integrations as indicated by the formulas of Table A.4, yields the following results:

$$w_b = \mp \int_0^L kQ \frac{L^2}{2} \sin^2 \alpha \, dl = \mp kQ \frac{L^3}{6} \sin^2 \alpha$$

$$w_{aa} = -aw_a + w'_{aa}$$

$$\text{where } w'_{aa} = \mp \int_0^L kQ \left( \frac{L}{2} - l \right) \frac{l^2}{2} \sin^2 \alpha \, dl$$

$$= \pm kQ \frac{L^4}{24} \cos \alpha \sin^2 \alpha$$

$$w_{bb} = +bw_b + w'_{bb}$$

where $w'_{bb} = \mp \int_0^L kQ \frac{L^2}{2} \sin^2 \alpha \, dl$

$$= \pm kQ \frac{L^4}{24} \sin^2 \alpha$$

The upper signs apply when $\sin \alpha$ is positive ($0 < \alpha < \pi$); the lower signs when $\sin \alpha$ is negative ($\pi < \alpha < 2\pi$).

For straight members in the p-plane acted upon by *wind* along the z (horizontal) axis, the identical formulas apply because of cyclic permutation.

![Fig. A.18 Integration of shape coefficients for straight members in the p-plane acted upon by z-wind.](figures/MWK_1956_p0322_fig02_fig-a-18-integration-of-shape-coefficien.png)

$$l' = l \cos \alpha \text{ when } -\frac{\pi}{2} < \alpha < \frac{\pi}{2}$$

$$= -l \cos \alpha \text{ when } \frac{\pi}{2} < \alpha < \frac{3\pi}{2}$$

$$x = a + \tfrac{1}{2}(L - 2l) \cos \alpha$$

$$y = b$$

$$z = c + \tfrac{1}{2}(L - 2l) \sin \alpha$$

$$l' = c + \tfrac{1}{2}(L - l) \sin \alpha$$

For straight members in the p-plane acted upon by a wind parallel to the x (vertical) axis, shown in Fig. A.18, it is necessary to derive the coefficients $w_a$, $w_{aa}$, and $w_{ab}$.

$$w_a = \mp \int_0^L kQ \frac{L^2}{2} \cos^2 \alpha \, dl = \pm kQ \frac{L^3}{6} \cos^2 \alpha$$

$$w_{ab} = +b w_{ab} + w'_{ab}$$

$$\text{where } w'_{ab} = \pm \int_0^L kQ \left( \frac{L}{2} - l \right) \frac{l^2}{2} \cos^2 \alpha \, dl$$

$$= \mp kQ \frac{L^4}{24} \sin \alpha \cos^2 \alpha$$

$$w_{aa} = -a w_a + w'_{aa}$$

$$\text{where } w'_{aa} = \mp \int_0^L kQ \left( \frac{L}{2} - l \right) \frac{l^2}{2} \cos^2 \alpha \, dl$$

$$= \pm kQ \frac{L^4}{24} \cos^3 \alpha$$

The upper signs apply when $\cos \alpha$ is positive ($-\pi/2 < \alpha < \pi/2$); lower signs when $\cos \alpha$ is negative ($\pi/2 < \alpha < 3\pi/2$).

For straight members in the p-plane acted upon by *wind* along the z-axis, the identical formulas apply.

---

![Fig. A.19 System of quadrants for circular members.](figures/MWK_1956_p0323_fig01_system-of-quadrants-for-circular-members.png)

The shape coefficients of circular members are given below. The signs to be used in the expressions which follow are dependent upon the location of the arc $R\phi$ in a system of quadrants which is oriented from the negative vertical axis as shown in Fig. A.19.

In deriving the shape coefficient formulas for circular members subjected to *in-plane* wind, the case of the member in the *x*-plane acted upon by *x* wind parallel to the *x*-axis is considered first. Figure A.20 shows such a member set up for integration in a *counterclockwise* direction.

![Fig. A.20 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for circular members in the x-plane acted upon by x-wind.](figures/MWK_1956_p0323_fig02_counterclockwise-integration-of-shape-co.png)

$$l' = \int_0^\phi dl' = \pm R [\cos \alpha - \cos (\alpha + \phi)]$$
$$dl' = \sin (\alpha + \phi) R \, d\phi$$
$$x = a + R \sin (\alpha + \phi)$$
$$y = b - R \cos (\alpha + \phi)$$
$$y' = b - \frac{1}{2}R[\cos \alpha + \cos (\alpha + \phi)]$$

$$w_b = \pm \int_0^\phi kQR^3 \frac{[\cos \alpha - \cos (\alpha + \phi)]^2}{2} d\phi$$

$$= \pm kQR^3 \left[ \frac{\Phi}{4} (2 + \cos 2\alpha) + \frac{\sin 2(\alpha + \Phi)}{8} - \cos \alpha \sin(\alpha + \Phi) + \tfrac{3}{8} \sin 2\alpha \right]$$

$$w_{ba} = -aw_b + w'_{ba}$$

where
$$w'_{ba} = \pm \int_0^\Phi kQR^4 \sin(\alpha + \phi) \frac{[\cos \alpha - \cos(\alpha + \phi)]^2}{2} d\phi = \pm kQR^4 \frac{[\cos \alpha - \cos \Phi]^3}{6}$$

$$w_{bb} = +bw_b + w'_{bb}$$

where
$$w'_{bb} = \pm \int_0^\Phi kQR^4 \cos(\alpha + \phi) \frac{[\cos \alpha - \cos(\alpha + \phi)]^2}{2} d\phi$$

$$= \pm kQR^4 \left[ \frac{\sin^3(\alpha + \Phi) - \sin^3 \alpha}{6} - \frac{\sin(\alpha + \Phi) - \sin \alpha}{2} \right.$$

$$\left. + \frac{\cos \alpha}{2} \{\Phi + \sin(\alpha + \Phi)\cos(\alpha + \Phi) - \sin(\alpha + \Phi)\cos \alpha\} \right]$$

The upper signs apply when $\Phi$ lies in the *I* and/or the *II* quadrants; the lower signs apply when $\Phi$ lies in the *III* and/or the *IV* quadrants. When $\Phi$ lies in the *I* and *IV* quadrants or the *II* and *III*, it must be split up into two arcs.

For the counterclockwise integration of circular members in the *y*-plane subjected to *x*-wind, the identical formulas apply.

---

![Fig. A.21 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for circular members in the y-plane acted upon by z-wind.](figures/MWK_1956_p0324_fig01_counterclockwise-integration-of-shape-co.png)

$$l' = \int_0^\phi dl' = \pm R \left[\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha\right]$$

$$dl' = \cos(\alpha + \phi) R \, d\alpha$$

$$x = b - R \cos \alpha$$

$$z = a + R \sin(\alpha + \phi)$$

$$z' = a + \tfrac{1}{2} R \left[\sin(\alpha + \phi) + \sin \alpha\right]$$

Fig. A.21 Counterclockwise integration of shape coefficients for circular members in the y-plane acted upon by z-wind.

The case of the circular member in the y-plane acted upon by a wind parallel to the x-axis is now considered. Figure A.21 shows such a member set up for integration in a *counterclockwise* direction.

$$w_{ax} = \mp \int_0^\phi kQR^3 \frac{[\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha]^2}{2} d\phi$$

$$= \mp k QR^3 \left[\frac{\Phi}{4}(2 - \cos 2\alpha) - \frac{\sin 2(\alpha + \Phi)}{8} + \sin \alpha \cos(\alpha + \Phi) - \tfrac{3}{4} \sin 2\alpha\right]$$

$$w_{ab} = + b w_a + w'_{ab}$$

where

$$w'_{ab} = \pm \int_0^\phi kQR^4 \cos(\alpha + \phi) \frac{[\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha]^2}{2} d\phi = \pm kQR^4 \frac{[\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha]^3}{6}$$

$$w_{az} = -aw_a + w'_{az}$$

where

$$w'_{az} = \pm \int_0^\phi kQR^4 \sin(\alpha + \phi) \frac{[\sin(\alpha + \phi) - \sin \alpha]^2}{2} d\phi$$

$$= \pm kQR^4 \left[\frac{\cos^3(\alpha + \phi) - \cos^3 \alpha}{6} - \frac{\cos(\alpha + \phi) - \cos \alpha}{2}\right]$$

$$- \frac{\sin \alpha}{2} \left[\Phi + \sin(\alpha + \Phi) \cos(\alpha + \Phi) + \sin \alpha \cos(\alpha + \Phi)\right]$$

The upper signs apply when $\Phi$ lies in the *I* and/or *IV* quadrant, the lower signs when $\Phi$ lies in the *II* and/or *III* quadrants. When $\Phi$ lies in the *I* and *II* quadrants or the *III* and *IV*, it must be split up into two arcs.

For the counterclockwise integration of circular members in the x-plane subjected to z-wind, the same formulas apply.

| $+B_{xy}$ | $+B_{yy}$ | $+B_{zy}$ | $+C_{xy}$ | $+C_{yy}$ | $+C_{zy}$ | $=$ | $+EI(\delta^*{}_y - \Delta_{yL}) = +EI(\delta_{yL} - x_N\delta_{xN} - \delta_{yO'} - \Delta_y)$ |
| $+B_{xz}$ | $+B_{yz}$ | $+B_{zz}$ | $+C_{xz}$ | $+C_{yz}$ | $+C_{zz}$ | $=$ | $+EI(\delta^*{}_z - \Delta_{zL}) = +EI(\delta_{zL} - \delta_{zO'} - \Delta_z)$ |

Up to this point, the development of the General Analytical Method has been built around the general case of the weightless pipe line subjected to loading which is concentrated at a point, or uniformly distributed over a number. Such a loading may arise from the weight of the piping components. Weight effects are not ordinarily of great significance although they become important when dealing with materials of low breaking strength or poor creep resistance, that is, if premature fracture or excessive sagging is not to be tolerated. The general formulas derived, however, are readily adapted to the evaluation of the effects of thermal expansion loading which are usually of primary interest.

Under thermal expansion, the strain energy is supplied by the temperature change involved; there are no applied loads, hence the load terms in the general equations of Table A.3 become zero leaving a system of equations which expresses the reactions in terms of imagined displacements of one end, designated the "free" end.$^4$ If $\Delta_x$, $\Delta_y$, $\Delta_z$, and $\Delta_x$ are the free thermal expansions, directed from the end designated fixed toward that designated free, they will enter the right-hand member of the equations with a negative$^5$ sign as indicated in Table A.5. Displacements of the ends, denoted $\delta^*{}_x$, $\delta^*{}_y$, $\delta^*{}_z$, which are due to movement of connected equipment, are entered with sign unchanged, so as to indicate the direction of the relative movement of the free end with respect to the fixed end. The angular displacements or rotations, $\theta_x$, $\theta_y$, $\theta_z$, are ordinarily assumed to be zero. For a pipe line with two fixed ends, the equations in six unknowns remain so that the problem can be solved by various numerical methods.

The components of rotation and deflection ($\theta_{xN}$, etc.) at any point $N$ on the pipe line are obtained—

$^4$Even though in actuality both ends are completely fixed, the action of thermal expansion may be visualized most conveniently by imagining a fictitious case where one end first expands without restraint and is subsequently restored by means of the reactions to the position dictated by end constraint.

$^5$The negative sign is needed since the restraining displacement is in the opposite direction to the free thermal expansion.

tained by substitution of the moment and force components determined above, back into the same relationships given in Table A.5 with the exception that integration limits are from $N$ to $O'$ and the constants are expressed as in Table A.6.

$+EI\theta_{yN}$
$+EI\theta_{zN}$
$+EI(\delta_{xN} - \Delta_{xN} + y_N\theta_{zN} - z_N\theta_{yN} - \delta_{xO'})$
$+EI(\delta_{yN} - \Delta_{yN} + z_N\theta_{xN} - x_N\theta_{zN} - \delta_{yO'})$
$+EI(\delta_{zN} - \Delta_{zN} + x_N\theta_{yN} - y_N\theta_{xN} - \delta_{zO'})$

Also, it can be seen that for convenience or for checking purposes, the integrations may be taken from $A$ to $N$ in which case the constants are as shown in Table A.7. It will be noted that the sums of the constants in Tables A.6 and A.7 are equal to the respective constants given in Table A.5.

The loading case of any *concentrated force* applied at a point $N$ on the pipe line of Fig. A.1 can be obtained from the general equations given in Table A.3 by considering the total load on the member $NF$ to remain unchanged while its length is made infinitely small. In this case, the shape coefficients in the columns headed by $w_x$, $w_y$, and $w_z$ vanish; the coefficients $\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$, $\bar{z}$ become $x_N$, $y_N$, $z_N$ respectively; the moments $M_{xN}$, $M_{yN}$, $M_{zN}$ are those at the origin due to the applied concentrated loads $F_{xN}$, $F_{yN}$, $F_{zN}$; and the system of equations appears as shown in the first six rows of Table A.8. When $F_{xN}$, $F_{yN}$, $F_{zN}$ are known loads the solution is obvious. When these forces are unknown, such as the reactions at

$+EI(-\theta_{yN})$
$+EI(-\theta_{zN})$
$+EI(\delta_{xN} - \delta_{xN} - \Delta_x + \Delta_{xN} - y_N\theta_{zN} + z_N\theta_{yN})$
$+EI(\delta_{yN} - \delta_{yN} - \Delta_y + \Delta_{yN} - z_N\theta_{xN} + x_N\theta_{zN})$
$+EI(\delta_{zN} - \delta_{zN} - \Delta_z + \Delta_{zN} - x_N\theta_{yN} + y_N\theta_{xN})$

HISTORY AND DERIVATION OF PIPING FLEXIBILITY ANALYSIS 325

stops, it is necessary to introduce additional equations in order to obtain a solution.

Referring again to Table A.8, the lower six equations, derived from Table A.6, relate the various reacting forces and moments to the rotations and deflections at point $N$. Since there is no external moment at point $N$:

$$M_{xN} = F_{aN}y_N - F_{yN}x_N$$
$$M_{yN} = F_{zN}x_N - F_{xN}z_N \tag{A.15}$$
$$M_{zN} = F_{yN}z_N - F_{zN}y_N$$

Furthermore, the deflections of the supports, stops, etc. $\delta_{xN}$, $\delta_{yN}$, $\delta_{zN}$ are expressable in terms of the forces which produce them, $F_{xN}$, $F_{yN}$, $F_{zN}$ (for the usual rigid supports, $\delta_{xN}$, $\delta_{yN}$, $\delta_{zN}$ are commonly taken equal to zero). Hence, the 12 equations of Table A.8 contain but 12 unknowns and consequently can be solved.

In the case of a branch line $BN$ connected to the main point $N$ as shown in Fig. A.22, the rotations, $\theta_{xN}$, $\theta_{yN}$, $\theta_{zN}$, as well as the deflections, $\delta_{xN}$, $\delta_{yN}$, $\delta_{zN}$, are affected by the flexibility of the branch. Thus the rotations at point $N$ cannot be considered unrestrained as they were in the treatment of stops. The junction moments in the branch at point $N$, $M'_{xN}$, $M'_{yN}$, $M'_{zN}$, expressed in terms of the terminal moments,$^b$ $M_{xB}$, $M_{yB}$, $M_{zB}$, are given by:

$$M'_{xN} = M_{xB} + F_{yB}z_N - F_{zB}y_N$$
$$M'_{yN} = M_{yB} + F_{zB}x_N - F_{xB}z_N \tag{A.16}$$
$$M'_{zN} = M_{zB} + F_{xB}y_N - F_{yB}x_N$$

$^b$ Referred to the origin.

![Fig. A.22 Three-anchor configuration.](figures/MWK_1956_p0326_fig01_three-anchor-configuration.png)

In the development of Table A.8, the moments $M_{AN}$, $M_{yN}$, $M_{zN}$, were understood to result only from *forces* applied at point $N$ since it was assumed that at that point no external moments were applied so that rotations were unrestrained. Consideration of the more general case leads to redefinition of the moment equations (A.15) as follows:

$$M_{xN} = M'_{xN} + F_{zN}y_N - F_{yN}z_N$$
$$M_{yN} = M'_{yN} + F_{xN}z_N - F_{zN}x_N \tag{A.17}$$
$$M_{zN} = M'_{zN} + F_{yN}x_N - F_{xN}y_N$$

But $F_{xN} = F_{xB}$, $F_{yN} = F_{yB}$, $F_{zN} = F_{zB}$, therefore, $M'_{xN} = M_{xB}$, $M'_{yN} = M_{yB}$, $M'_{zN} = M_{zB}$. Hence, with appropriate changes to the subscripts and limits of Table A.8 the 12 equations for the branched system are derived, appearing as shown in Table A.9.

The influence of normal forces and shears is negligible in most piping calculations except that on rare occasions for thermal expansion effects it may warrant investigation. Hence, the development of these constants is given only for the case of concentrated loads (or thermal expansion).

The energy of shear is given by the following:

$$U_s = \int_0^L \frac{k_s \lambda F_s^2 \, dl}{2GA} \tag{A.18}$$

and the energy of normal force be

$$U_n = \int_0^l \frac{k_n F_n^2 \, dl}{2EA} \quad (A.19)$$

where $A_k$ = flexibility factor in shear = 1.

$\lambda$ = shear distribution factor which depends on the shape of the cross section ( = 2 for thin-walled cylinders).

$F_t$ = shearing force.

$A$ = cross-sectional area.

$k_n$ = flexibility factor in tension or compression = 1.

$F_n$ = normal force.

The shear equation may be written

$$U_s = \int_0^l \left( \frac{F_t^2 + F'_t{}^2}{GA} \right) dl \quad (A.20)$$

where shearing force is expressed in components $F_s$ and $F'_s$, respectively in and transverse to a reference plane containing the particular portion of the line.

If the subside, inside, and mean radii of the pipe cross section are designated by $r_o$, $r_i$, $r_m$ respectively, and the wall thickness by $t$, the properties of the section and their approximate relationship may be expressed as follows:

$$A = \pi(r_o^2 - r_i^2) = 2\pi r_m t$$

$$I = \frac{\pi}{4}(r_o^4 - r_i^4) = \pi r_m^3 t$$

$$\frac{I}{A} = \frac{r_m^2}{2}$$

Substituting these values into eqs. A.19 and A.20

and introducing the stiffness factor $Q$, the total energy due to shear and normal forces becomes

$$U_{sn} = \frac{1}{2EI} \int Q(2.6F_t^2 + 2.6F'_t{}^2 + 0.5F_n^2) r_m^2 \, dl \quad (A.21)$$

Applying Castigliano's theorem, the displacement in the z-direction is given by

$$\delta_z = \frac{1}{EI} \int_0^l Q r_m^2 \left( 2.6F_s \frac{\partial F_s}{\partial F_z} + 2.6F'_s \frac{\partial F'_s}{\partial F_z} + 0.5F_n \frac{\partial F_n}{\partial F_z} \right) dl \quad (A.22)$$

Similar equations can be written for $\delta_y$ and $\delta_x$ by substituting for $\partial F_z$ the partial differential of the applicable force.

The shear and normal forces for any point in the z-plane are

$$F_s = F_x \cos \psi - F_y \sin \psi$$
$$F'_s = F_z$$
$$F_n = F_y \cos \psi + F_x \sin \psi$$

Similarly for any point in the y-plane

$$F_s = F_x \cos \phi - F_z \sin \phi$$
$$F'_s = F_y$$
$$F_n = F_z \cos \phi + F_x \sin \phi$$

and for any point in the x-plane

$$F_s = F_y \cos \theta - F_z \sin \theta$$
$$F'_s = F_x$$
$$F_n = F_z \cos \theta + F_y \sin \theta$$

# APPENDIX

# B

# Derivation of Acoustic Vibration Formulas

IN Chapter 9, the derivations of certain expressions were omitted because of their length. As they are not available in the literature, at least not in the form given herein, they are included in this appendix. Numbered citations below refer to the list of references at the end of Chapter 9.

## B.1 Multiple Resonator of nth Order

General expressions for the natural frequencies of multiple resonator systems can be derived and will be given here for the sake of completeness (see also [24]). Consider Fig. B.1. $V$ (ft), $A$ (ft$^2$), $L$ (ft) are chamber volume, neck area, and neck length respectively. In addition let:

Acoustic conductivity $= \mu = \dfrac{A}{L + \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi A}}$ (ft);

$C =$ speed of sound in fluid (ft/sec)

Then,

$$f = \frac{C}{2\pi}\sqrt{\eta} \qquad \text{(B.1)}$$

where $\eta$ is a root of the determinantal equation:

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\dfrac{1}{V_1} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_1} \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_1} \,, & 0 \,, & 0 \,, & \cdots & 0 \,, & 0 \\[6pt]
-\dfrac{1}{V_1} \,, & \dfrac{1}{V_1} + \dfrac{1}{V_2} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_2} \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_2} \,, & 0 \,, & \cdots & 0 \,, & 0 \\[6pt]
0 \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_2} \,, & \dfrac{1}{V_2} + \dfrac{1}{V_3} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_3} \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_3} \,, & \cdots & 0 \,, & 0 \\[6pt]
0 \,, & 0 \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_3} \,, & \dfrac{1}{V_3} + \dfrac{1}{V_4} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_4} \,, & \cdots & 0 \,, & 0 \\[6pt]
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\[6pt]
\dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_1 V_n} \,, & \dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_2 V_n} \,, & \dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_3 V_n} \,, & \dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_4 V_n} \,, & \cdots & \dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_{n-1} V_n} \,, & \dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_n V_n} - \dfrac{\eta}{V_{n-1}} + \dfrac{1}{V_n} - \dfrac{\eta}{V_n}
\end{vmatrix} = 0
$$

This result was derived on the basis of a generalization of the method of derivation given by Rayleigh in the "Theory of Sound," Vol. II [3], for $n = 1, 2$; the $n$ roots of the determinantal equation are all real and positive, corresponding to $n$ physical modes.

For $n = 1$ $V_1 = V$, $(V_2 = \cdots = V_n = \infty)$ is found the following:

$$\dfrac{\mu_{n+1}}{\mu_n V_n} + \dfrac{1}{V_{n-1}} - \dfrac{\eta}{V_n} + 0 + \dfrac{1}{V_1} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_1} = 0 \qquad \text{(B.3)}$$

or

$$\eta = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1}, \qquad f = \frac{C}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1}} \qquad \text{(B.4)}$$

and for $\mu_2 = 0$, (2nd neck closed)

$$f = \frac{C}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_1}{V_1}} \qquad \text{(B.5)}$$

For $n = 2$ the determinantal reduces to:

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\dfrac{1}{V_1} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_1} \,, & -\dfrac{1}{V_1} \\[6pt]
\dfrac{\mu_3}{\mu_1 V_2} - \dfrac{1}{V_1} \,, & \dfrac{\mu_3}{\mu_2 V_2} + \dfrac{1}{V_1} + \dfrac{1}{V_2} - \dfrac{\eta}{\mu_2}
\end{vmatrix} = 0 \qquad \text{(B.6)}$$

---

## DERIVATION OF ACOUSTIC VIBRATION FORMULAS

From which:

$$\eta^2 - \left(\frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1} + \frac{\mu_2 + \mu_3}{V_2}\right)\eta \quad \text{(B.7)}$$

$$+ \frac{\mu_1 \cdot \mu_3 + \mu_2 \cdot \mu_3 + \mu_1 \cdot \mu_2}{V_1 V_2} = 0$$

So that

$$f = \frac{C}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1} + \frac{\mu_2 + \mu_3}{V_2}\right)}$$

$$\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1} + \frac{\mu_2 + \mu_3}{V_2}\right)^2 - \frac{\mu_1 \mu_3 + \mu_2 \mu_3 (\mu_1 + \mu_2)}{V_1 V_2}} \quad \text{(B.8)}$$

For $n = 3$, let:

$$\alpha_1 = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{V_1} + \frac{\mu_2 + \mu_3}{V_2} + \frac{\mu_3 + \mu_4}{V_3}$$

$$\alpha_2 = \frac{\mu_1 \mu_3 (\mu_2 + \mu_3) + \mu_2 \mu_3 \mu_4}{V_1 V_2} + \frac{(\mu_1 + \mu_2)(\mu_3 + \mu_4)}{V_1 V_3} \quad \text{(B.9)}$$

$$+ \frac{\mu_2 \mu_3 \cdot (\mu_2 + \mu_4)(\mu_1 + \mu_2)}{V_2 V_3}$$

$$\alpha_3 = \frac{\mu_1 \mu_3 (\mu_2 + \mu_4) + \mu_2 \mu_4 (\mu_1 + \mu_2)}{V_1 V_2 V_3}$$

Then

$$f = \frac{C}{2\pi} \sqrt{\eta}$$

with $\eta$ being a root of:

$$\eta_3 - \alpha_1 \eta^2 + \alpha_2 \eta - \alpha_3 = 0 \quad \text{(B.10)}$$

The 3 roots of the cubic equation are real and positive, corresponding to 3 physical modes.

In particular, if all chamber volumes, neck lengths, and areas are equal thus

$$f = \frac{C}{\pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{V}} \times \sin\left(\frac{m\pi}{8}\right) \quad \text{(B.11)}$$

$$m = 1, 2, 3$$

A more general result for $n$ resonators of equal volumes, areas, and lengths is:

$$f_m = \frac{a}{\pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{V}} \cdot \frac{m\pi}{2(n+1)} \quad \text{(B.12)}$$

$$m = 1, 2, \ldots n$$

which is the same result as given in reference [24], eq. 19, except that in that equation there is an error and *n* should have been printed instead of *m* in the denominator of the argument of $\sin\left(\frac{m}{m+1}\pi\right)$

![Fig. B.1 Multiple resonator.](figures/MWK_1956_p0330_fig01_fig-b-1-multiple-resonator.png)

Finally it may be added that the results also apply if the configuration of resonators, while in series, is not in a straight-line direction.

### B.2 General Characteristic Equation for a Branched Piping System

The hydrodynamic equations of motion for one-dimensional non-steady flow without friction or heat transfer are:

$$\rho \frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \rho U \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} \quad \text{(momentum)}$$

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\rho U) = 0 \quad \text{(continuity)}$$

where $\rho$, $p$, $U$ are pressure, density, and velocity respectively. In addition, for an isentropic process for a gas.

$$p = \text{Const.} \, \rho^\gamma \qquad (\gamma = C_p / C_v)$$

If barred symbols represent mean values, while $\Delta$'s represent increments, then the equations assume the form:

$$(\bar{\rho} + \Delta \rho) \frac{\partial (\bar{U} + \Delta U)}{\partial t} + (\bar{\rho} + \Delta \rho)(\bar{U} + \Delta U) \frac{\partial (\bar{U} + \Delta U)}{\partial x}$$

$$= -\frac{\partial (\bar{p} + \Delta p)}{\partial x}$$

$$\frac{\partial (\Delta \rho)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (\Delta \rho)}{\partial x} (\bar{U} + \Delta U) + (\bar{\rho} + \Delta \rho) \frac{\partial (\Delta U)}{\partial x} = 0$$

$$\bar{p} + \Delta p = \gamma \frac{\bar{p}}{\bar{\rho}} \Delta \rho = \bar{p} + C^2 \Delta \rho$$

$$C = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma \bar{p}}{\bar{\rho}}} = \text{speed of sound, considered constant.}$$

Subtracting the mean values, considering the $\Delta$'s infinitesimal and neglecting terms of higher order than 1st in the infinitesimals:

$$\bar{\rho} \frac{\partial (\Delta U)}{\partial t} + \bar{\rho} \bar{U} \frac{\partial (\Delta U)}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial (\Delta p)}{\partial x}$$

$$\frac{\partial (\Delta \rho)}{\partial t} + \bar{U} \frac{\partial (\Delta \rho)}{\partial x} + \bar{\rho} \frac{\partial (\Delta U)}{\partial x} = 0$$

$$\Delta p = C^2 \Delta \rho$$

---

Suppose now infinitesimal perturbations relative to a quiescent state, i.e. $\bar{U} = 0$. Eliminating $\Delta\rho$ via the 3rd relation gives:

$$\bar{p} \frac{\partial(\Delta U)}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial(\Delta p)}{\partial x}$$

$$\bar{p} \frac{\partial(\Delta U)}{\partial x} = -\frac{1}{C^2} \frac{\partial(\Delta p)}{\partial t}$$

(B.13a)

From which, by further differentiation:

$$\frac{\partial^2(\Delta U)}{\partial x^2} = \frac{1}{C^2} \frac{\partial^2(\Delta U)}{\partial t^2}$$

$$\frac{\partial^2(\Delta p)}{\partial x^2} = \frac{1}{C^2} \frac{\partial^2(\Delta p)}{\partial t^2}$$

(B.13b)

Equations B.13b are the familiar wave equations for one dimensional velocity, governing the propagation of small (infinitesimal) disturbances in a fluid medium ($C =$ speed of "sound" = speed of propagation of infinitesimal disturbances).

Particular solutions of the wave equation are obtained by separation of variables. Thus if:

$$\Delta p = f_1(x) f_2(t)$$

Then

$$f_2(t) \frac{d^2 f_1}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{C^2} f_1(x) \frac{d^2 f_2}{dt^2}$$

Or

$$\frac{1}{f_1} \frac{d^2 f_1}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{C^2} \frac{1}{f_2} \frac{d^2 f_2}{dt^2} = -\lambda^2$$

Since $f_1$ is a function of $x$ only and $f_2$ is a function only of $t$, $\lambda$ must be a function of neither, i.e. a constant.

The solutions for $f_1$ and $f_2$ must be of the form:

$$f_1(x) = B_1 \cos \lambda x + B_2 \sin \lambda x$$

$$f_2(t) = D_1 \cos \lambda C t + D_2 \sin \lambda C t$$

An equivalent form of the solution is also:

$$\Delta p = E_1 \cos\left(\frac{\omega x}{C} + \phi\right) e^{i\omega t}; \quad \omega = \lambda C; \quad i = \sqrt{-1}$$

Likewise, by analogous reasoning:

$$\Delta(\bar{p}U) = E_2 \cos\left(\frac{\omega x}{C} + \phi_2\right) e^{i\omega t}$$

However, $E_1$, $E_2$, $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are not completely independent of one another, since the solution must also satisfy equations B.13a. It can be verified by direct substitution that the forms:

$$\Delta p = i C R \cos\left(\frac{\omega x}{C} + \phi\right) e^{i\omega t}$$

$$\Delta(\bar{p}U) = R \sin\left(\frac{\omega x}{C} + \phi\right) e^{i\omega t}$$

(B.13c)

satisfy not only the wave equations B.13b but also equations B.13a, and hence represent a solution of both systems of partial differential equations. $R$ is in general a "complex amplitude," while $\phi$ is, of course, a real quantity.

**Boundary Conditions at a Junction.** The boundary conditions at any junction are given by continuity of both pressure and mass flow rate. Thus at any junction of $n$ branches or segments, for pressure continuity:

$$i C R_1 \cos\left(\frac{\omega L_1 x_1}{C} + \phi_1\right) = i C R_2 \cos\left(\frac{\omega L_2 x_2}{C} + \phi_2\right)$$

$$= \cdots = i C R_n \cos\left(\frac{\omega L_n x_n}{C} + \phi_n\right)$$

(B.13d)

where $L_1 x_1$, $L_2 x_2$, ... $L_n x_n$ were defined previously. While for continuity of mass flow rate:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \pm a_i R_i \sin\left(\frac{\omega L_i x_i}{C} + \phi_i\right) = 0$$

(B.13e)

the $a$'s being the areas and the ($\pm$) sign to be taken as defined previously.

Substituting Eqs. B.13d into B.13e yields:

$$R_i \cos\left(\frac{\omega L_i x_i}{C} + \phi_i\right) \sum_{i=1}^{n} \pm a_i \tan\left(\frac{\omega L_i x_i}{C} + \phi_i\right) = 0$$

Or, assuming the 1st factor $\neq 0$, then

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \pm a_i \tan\left(\frac{\omega L_i x_i}{C} + \phi_i\right) = 0$$

Now

$$\frac{\omega L_i x_i}{C} = \frac{2\pi f_0 L_i x_i}{C/L} = \frac{2\pi f}{f_0} \cdot \frac{L_i x_i}{L}; \quad f_0 = \frac{C}{4L}$$

and writing $\beta_i$ instead of $\phi_i$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \pm a_i \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \frac{f}{f_0} \cdot \frac{L_i x_i}{L} + \beta_i\right) = 0$$

(B.13f)

which is the result given in the text above.

---

**End Conditions**

a. Intake point, $z = 0$

Node

At a node, $\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t} = 0$

From eq. B.13c:

$i\omega R \sin \phi e^{i\omega t} = 0$

or

$\phi = \beta = 0$

Loop

$\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial t} = 0$

Hence from eq. B.13c

$-\omega C R \cos \phi e^{i\omega t} = 0$

or

$\phi = \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

b. Discharge point, $z = L$

Node

$i\omega R \sin\left(\dfrac{\omega L}{C} + \phi\right) e^{i\omega t} = 0$

or

$\sin\left(\dfrac{\omega L}{C} + \phi\right) = 0$

$\phi = \beta = m\pi - \dfrac{\omega L}{C} = m\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\dfrac{f}{f_0} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(2m - \dfrac{f}{f_0}\right)$

$m = 0, 1, 2, \cdots;$

$m = 0$ is trivial solution (quiescent).

$m = 1$ is fundamental.

$m = 2$ is 1st harmonic, etc.

Loop

$\cos\dfrac{\omega L}{C} = 0; \phi = \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{2} \cdots = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\dfrac{f}{f_0}\left(m - \dfrac{f}{f_0}\right)$

$m = 1, 3, 5 \cdots$

corresponding to fundamental, 1st harmonic, etc., which are the results given previously in the text (Subsection 9.6c).

## B.3 Tuned Resonator Relations

Consider the schematic below representing a piping system with a (tuned) resonator and orifice (Fig. B.2). The entire pressure loss in the pipe may be considered as an orifice effect. This is the case which will be elucidated in somewhat more detail later.

![Fig. B.2 Tuned resonator](figures/MWK_1956_p0332_fig01_fig-b-2-tuned-resonator.png)

Let bars represent mean values while $\Delta$'s represent increments. Thus let the mean values of flow rate, pressure and density be $\overline{Q}$, $\overline{p}$, $\overline{\rho}$. Let the incremental values of flow rates and pressures be: $\Delta Q$, $\Delta Q_1$, $\Delta Q_2$ (as indicated on the schematic), $\Delta p_1$, and $\Delta p_2$. In accordance with procedure that a certain amount of mass oscillates as a rigid body in the neck; let the effective length of this mass column be $L^* = L + \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi A}$ where $L$ and $A$ are the length and cross-sectional area of the neck, and suppose that at a given instance this mass penetrates the resonator chamber a distance $z$, measured from an initial position. The distance $z$ is supposed to be small, of the same order as the increments. Then:

$$\Delta Q_2 = (\overline{p} + \Delta p_1) A \dot{z} = A \dot{z} \quad \text{(B.14)}$$

From the equilibrium of the vibrating mass:

$$\overline{\rho} L L^* \ddot{z} + A \Delta p_2 = A (\Delta p_1) \quad \text{(B.15)}$$

and:

$$\Delta Q_2 = V \overline{\rho} \dot{z} = \dfrac{V}{C^2} \dot{p}_2 = \dfrac{V}{C^2} (\Delta \dot{p}_2) \quad \text{(B.16)}$$

where $C_2 = dp/d\rho$ = speed of sound, considered constant.

From B.14 and B.16:

$$\overline{\rho} A \dot{z} = \dfrac{V}{C^2} (\Delta \dot{p}_2) \quad \text{or} \quad (\Delta p_2) = \dfrac{C^2}{V} \overline{\rho} A \dot{z} \quad \text{(B.17)}$$

For a small pressure drop through the orifice we have

$\overline{Q} + \Delta Q_1 = k\sqrt{\overline{p} + \Delta p_1 - p_0}$

$= k\sqrt{\overline{p} - p_0}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta p_1}{\overline{p} - p_0}\right)$

While

$\overline{Q} = k\sqrt{\overline{p} - p_0}$

From which

$\dfrac{\Delta Q_1}{\overline{Q}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta p_1}{\overline{p} - p_0}$

---

So that

$$\Delta p_3 = \frac{2(\bar{p} - p_0)}{\bar{Q}} \Delta Q_1 = \frac{2 \Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{Q}} \Delta Q_1$$

Hence

$$\Delta \bar{p} = \bar{p} - p_0$$

$$(\Delta p_3)_1' = \frac{2 \Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{Q}} (\Delta Q_1) \quad (B.18)$$

Differentiating B.15, substituting B.17 and B.18, and simplifying:

$$\ddot{x} + \frac{C^2 A}{V L^2} \dot{x} - 2 \frac{\Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{p} L^2} \left( \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}} \right) = 0 \quad (B.19)$$

Also from continuity:

$$\frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}} + \frac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}} = \frac{\Delta Q}{\bar{Q}}$$

Or substituting from B.14:

$$\frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}} + \frac{\dot{x} A}{\bar{Q}} \dot{x} = \frac{\Delta Q}{\bar{Q}} \quad (B.20)$$

Equations (B.19) and (B.20) are two linear differential equations in terms of $\Delta Q_1 / \bar{Q}$ and $x$, $\Delta Q / \bar{Q}$ being given as a function of time. For steady state harmonic oscillation let:

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{\bar{Q}} = R e^{i \omega t}, \quad \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}} = R_1 e^{i \omega t}, \quad x = x_0 e^{i \omega t}, \quad i = \sqrt{-1}$$

$R$, $R_1$, and $x_0$ being, in general, complex. Substituting in B.19 and B.20 gives, after some rearrangement:

$$(\omega^2 - \omega_n{}^2) x_0 + \frac{2 \Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{p} L^2} R_1 = 0 \quad (B.21)$$

$$R_1 + i \omega \frac{\bar{p} A}{\bar{Q}} x_0 = R \quad (B.22)$$

Where $\omega_n{}^2 = C^2 A / V L^2$ is the square of the resonator natural frequency, in accordance with the results given previously.

From B.21 and B.22:

$$\frac{R_1}{R} = \frac{1}{1 + \left[ \frac{2 A \Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{Q} L^2} \right] \omega} \cdot \frac{1}{(\omega_n{}^2 - \omega^2)} i$$

whence the magnification factor (M.F.) for $\Delta Q_1 / \bar{Q}$ becomes

$$\left| \frac{R_1}{R} \right| = \text{M.F.} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left[ \frac{\left( \frac{2 A \Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{Q} L^2} \right) \omega}{(\omega_n{}^2 - \omega^2)} \right]^2}} \quad (B.23)$$

Now let

$$\tau = \frac{2}{\bar{p}} \frac{\Delta \bar{p}}{\bar{Q}} \frac{V}{\bar{p}} \quad (B.24)$$

where

$$\bar{V} = \frac{V}{\bar{p}} = \text{average volume flow rate}$$

Then $\tau$ is a time constant of the resonator orifice combination, considered merely as a filter. Since $C^2 = \bar{p}/\bar{\rho}$ and $\omega_n{}^2 = C^2 A / V L^2$,

eq. B.23 gives the final expression for the magnification factor of $\Delta Q_1 / \bar{Q}$:

$$\text{M.F.} = \left| \frac{R_1}{R} \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left[ \frac{\tau \omega}{1 - (\omega/\omega_n)^2} \right]^2}} \quad (B.25)$$

It is seen from eq. B.24 that $\tau$ is proportional to the pressure drop across the orifice and the volume of the resonator. The greater the value of $\tau$ the smaller the M.F. and the better the smoothing. However, even for a very small value of $\tau$ (say a very small pressure drop across orifice), the magnification factor still tends to zero if the resonator frequency is *chosen so as to coincide with the forcing frequency $\omega$*. This then is the "tuning" phenomenon.

Since an ideal case is considered, the M.F. drops to zero at the tuning frequency. In a physical case this will not happen, of course, although in the neighborhood of the tuned frequency, the M.F. will drop sharply. The effect of the orifice pressure drop and resonator capacity, as reflected via the time constant $\tau$, is to maintain a lower value of the magnification factor in a *band* of frequencies around the tuned frequency; the larger $\tau$ the wider the band. If there exists no orifice, then instead of a concentrated pressure drop there will be a continuous pressure drop due to pipe friction. The smoothing will then occur in a finite length of pipe in the neighborhood of the resonator. A curve of the magnification factor for the outflow pulsations $\Delta Q_1 / \bar{Q}$ vs. $\omega/\omega_n$ is shown in Fig. B.4.

$$\tau = 1/\omega_n$$

Finally, from the previous results it is found that the magnification factor for the flow into the resonator

$$\left| \frac{\Delta Q_2 / \bar{Q}}{\Delta Q_1 / \bar{Q}} \right| = \left| \frac{R_2}{R} \right|$$

---

![Fig. B.3 Tuned resonator magnification factors.](figures/MWK_1956_p0334_fig01_fig-b-3-tuned-resonator-magnification-fa.png)

![Fig. B.4 Schematic of surge tank.](figures/MWK_1956_p0334_fig02_fig-b-4-schematic-of-surge-tank.png)

is given by

$$\left|\frac{R_2}{R}\right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left[\frac{1 - (\omega/\omega_n)^2}{r\omega}\right]^2}} \quad (B.26)$$

$\Delta Q_2/\bar{Q}$ is found to be 90° out of phase to $\Delta Q_1/\bar{Q}$, and the magnification of the former is a maximum (=1) when the M.F. of the latter is a minimum (=0) and vice versa. A curve of $|R_2/R|$ vs. $\omega/\omega_n$ for $r = 1/\omega_n$ is also shown in Fig. B.3. As appears from Fig. B.3, if $r$ is very small then for all forcing frequencies, except in the immediate neighborhood of the tuned frequency, the pulsations pass through unattenuated with the resonator quiescent. But, in the immediate neighborhood of the tuned frequency the situation is suddenly reversed, the outflow pulsations are attenuated while the resonator responds to the incoming pulsations. This represents the action of a tuned resonator.

## B.4 Simplified Surge Filter Analysis

Derivation of Results (see Fig. B.4).

Let $V$ = volume of tank, ft$^3$.

$a$ = effective orifice area, ft$^2$.

$Q_1(t)$ = mass flow rate from compressor, time variable, slugs/sec.

$Q_2(t)$ = mass flow rate from tank into piping system, time variable, slugs/sec.

$p(t)$ = pressure in tank, time variable, lbs/ft$^2$.

$p_0$ = pressure in pipe, considered constant, lbs/ft$^2$.

If smoothing is to be effective then the assumption that $p_0$ is constant will be valid.

$\rho(t)$ = density in tank, time variable, slugs/ft.

$T$ = temperature of gas in tank, degrees Rankine.

An *isothermal* process is assumed so that $T$ is constant.

$C$ = speed of sound, constant for an isothermal process, ft/sec.

$\bar{R}$ = gas constant, ft·lb/slugs $\times$ degrees F.

$\gamma$ = ratio of specific heats.

$$C = \sqrt{\gamma \bar{R} T} \quad (B.27)$$

It is assumed that the pressure drop across the effective orifice is moderate so that, at all times, the flow is well in the subsonic range. In this case, instead of the theoretically exact, but cumbersome, relation between pressure drop and flow rate through an orifice in the subsonic case, an approximate but simpler version of the Bernoulli type may be written:

$$Q_2(t) = a\sqrt{\rho(t)[p(t) - p_0]} \quad (B.28)$$

where $a$ = effective orifice area, including contraction coefficient, $\times \sqrt{2}$.

Then, by virtue of the gas law,

$$p = \bar{R}\rho T \quad (B.29)$$

and the definition of speed of sound $C$, eq. B.27,

$$Q_2(t) = \frac{a\sqrt{\gamma}}{C}\sqrt{p(t)[p(t) - p_0]} \quad (B.30)$$

From continuity:

$$Q_1(t) - Q_2(t) = V\dot{\rho}(t) \quad (B.31)$$

$$(\dot{\rho} = d\rho/dt)$$

But, on the assumption of an isothermal process,

$$\dot{\rho}(t) = \frac{\dot{p}(t)}{\bar{R}T} = \frac{\gamma}{C^2}\dot{p}(t) \quad (B.32)$$

Substituting the last result into eq. B.31 gives:

$$Q_1(t) - Q_2(t) = \frac{\gamma V}{C^2}\dot{p}(t) \quad (B.33)$$

---

Substituting now the expression for $Q_2(t)$ from eq. B.30 into eq. B.33 and dividing through by a factor yields the following:

$$\dot{p}(t) + \frac{aC}{\gamma V} \sqrt{p(t)[p(t) - p_0]} = \frac{C^2}{\gamma V} Q_1(t) \quad (B.34)$$

$Q_1(t)$, being the output from the compressor, is a known time function. Hence, eq. B.34 is a first order differential equation for the instantaneous tank pressure $p(t)$. This differential equation, however, is non-linear.

It is supposed now that the pulsations are moderate in amplitude relative to their average values. Let the average values, being time independent, be represented by bars above the corresponding symbols. Thus:

$$p(t) = \bar{p} + \Delta p; \quad \dot{p}(t) = \Delta \dot{p} = d(\Delta p)/dt$$
$$Q_1(t) = \bar{Q}_1 + \Delta Q_1 = \bar{Q}_1 + \Delta Q_1$$
$$Q_2(t) = \bar{Q}_2 + \Delta Q_2 = \bar{Q}_1 + \Delta Q_1 \quad \text{i.e., } \bar{Q}_1 = \bar{Q}_2$$

On the assumption that the increments $(\Delta\text{'s})$ are small, relative to the average values, the expression $\sqrt{p(t)[p(t) - p_0]}$ may be approximated by a binomial expansion to first order terms in the increment $\Delta p$, as follows:

$$\sqrt{p[p - p_0]} \approx \sqrt{\bar{p}(\bar{p} - p_0)} \left[1 + \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - p_0/\bar{p}} \cdot \frac{\Delta p}{\bar{p}}\right] \quad (B.35)$$

Also, in terms of the average values only, eq. B.34 reduces to:

$$\frac{a\sqrt{V}}{C} \sqrt{\bar{p}(\bar{p} - p_0)} = \bar{Q}_1 \quad (B.36)$$

By virtue of eqs. B.35 and B.36, eq. B.34 reduces, after some simplification, to:

$$\frac{\gamma V}{C^2} \bar{Q}_1 \left(\frac{\Delta \dot{p}}{\bar{p}}\right) + \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - p_0/\bar{p}} \cdot \frac{\Delta p}{\bar{p}} = \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} \quad (B.37)$$

Likewise, by virtue of eq. B.35, it follows from eq. B.30 that

$$\frac{\Delta p}{\bar{p}} = \frac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} \cdot \frac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}_2} \quad (B.38)$$

Substituting the last relation into eq. B.37 gives:

$$\frac{\gamma V}{C^2} \bar{Q}_1 \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} \left(\frac{\Delta \dot{Q}_2}{\bar{Q}_2}\right) + \frac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}_2} = \frac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} \quad (B.39)$$

Equation B.39 is a first order *linear* differential equation expressing the variation in outflow as a function of the variation in inflow (i.e. into the tank), relative to average values. If:

Inflow variation with respect to mean flow rate $\quad \dfrac{\Delta Q_1}{\bar{Q}_1} = x$

Outflow variation with respect to mean flow rate $\quad \dfrac{\Delta Q_2}{\bar{Q}_2} = y$

Time contact $\quad \dfrac{\gamma V}{C^2} \dfrac{\bar{Q}_1}{\bar{p}} \dfrac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} = \tau$

$$(B.40)$$

then eq. B.39 assumes the form:

$$\tau \dot{y} + y = x \quad (B.41)$$

The last first order linear non-homogeneous differential equation is the familiar differential equation of a first order filter, $\tau$ being the "time constant" of the filter, having the dimension of time.

Since,

$$C^2 = \gamma \bar{R} \bar{T} = \frac{\gamma \bar{p}}{\bar{\rho}}$$

Then, if

$$Q^*_1 = \frac{\bar{Q}_1}{\bar{\rho}}$$

represents the average volume flow rate, relative to average tank density per unit time, the expression for $\tau$ becomes:

$$\tau = \frac{V}{Q^*_1} \cdot \frac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}p_0/\bar{p}} \quad (B.42)$$

The output from a reciprocating compressor is pulse-like and all harmonics are contained in it. However, if the fundamental harmonic is attenuated by the filter, the higher harmonics can surely be disregarded and it is thus sufficient to consider $\Delta Q_1/\bar{Q}_1 = x$ of a purely sinusoidal form

$$x = x_0 e^{i\omega t}$$

Then the steady state solution for $y$ is of the form $y = y_0 e^{i\omega t}$, and from the differential eq. B.41:

$$y_0 (i\tau\omega + 1) = x_0 \quad (B.43)$$

The attenuation factor is the absolute value of the ratio $x_0/y_0$. Or,

$$\text{A.F} = \sqrt{1 + (\tau \omega)^2} \qquad i = \sqrt{-1} \quad (B.44)$$

Consider a reciprocating compressor, with $N = $ rpm and $m = $ number of cylinders, uniformly spacing of cylinders being assumed, then,

For single action,

$$\omega = 2\pi \frac{N}{60} m$$

---

## DERIVATION OF ACOUSTIC VIBRATION FORMULAS

For double action,

$$\omega = 4\pi \frac{N}{60} m \quad (B.45)$$

If then, $V^* =$ volume flow of gas per single stroke per piston, calculated relative to average *tank* density, it is found, by virtue of eqs. B.42 and B.45, that for either case:

$$v_w = 2\pi \frac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \frac{1}{2} p_0/\bar{p}} \frac{V}{V^*} \quad (B.46)$$

Finally, $p_0$ is the pressure immediately at the (effective) orifice. Actually, there is usually some pressure recovery. The latter varies with orifice-to-pipe diameter. A pressure recovery of 50% is assumed. If $(p_0/\bar{p})_a$ is the actual pressure ratio be-

tween tank and piping, then (for 50% pressure recovery):

$$(\bar{p} - p_0)_a = \tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{p} - p_0)$$

where $\bar{p}_a = \bar{p}$, hence,

$$\left(\frac{p_0}{\bar{p}}\right) = 2\left(\frac{p_0}{\bar{p}}\right)_a - 1$$

and

$$\frac{1 - p_0/\bar{p}}{1 - \tfrac{1}{2} p_0/\bar{p}} = \frac{1 - (p_0/\bar{p})_a}{\tfrac{3}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}(p_0/\bar{p})_a} \quad (B.47)$$

substituting eqs. B.46 and B.47 into eq. B.44, gives the final expression for the attenuation factor A.F.,

$$\text{A.F.} = \sqrt{1 + \left(2\pi \frac{1 - (p_0/\bar{p})_a}{\tfrac{3}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}(p_0/\bar{p})_a} \frac{V}{V^*}\right)^2} \quad (B.48)$$

The results are shown in Fig. 9.30 (Subsection 9.8b) for $(p_0/\bar{p})_a = 0.99, 0.95, 0.9, 0.8$.

## C-4. Chart for Criterion in Par. 620(a) in Code for Pressure Piping ASA B31.1

![C-4. Chart for Criterion in Par. 620\(a\) in Code for Pressure Piping ASA B31.1](figures/MWK_1956_p0344_fig01_c-4-chart-for-criterion-in-par-620-a-in.png)

$$\frac{U}{D} = \frac{\text{Anchor distance, ft}}{\text{Nominal diameter, in.}}$$

*Analysis of piping is mandatory if*

$$\frac{L}{U} < R'$$

$D$ = Nominal diameter of pipe, in.

$L$ = Developed pipe length, ft.

$Y$ = Resultant of restrained thermal expansion and net linear terminal displacements, in.

$U$ = Anchor distance (length of straight line joining anchors), ft.

$T$ = Temperature, F.

\* The temperature scale may be used instead of $Y/U$ when there is no displacement of the anchor points.

### Basis of Chart

Analysis of piping is mandatory if the following criterion is not satisfied:

$$\frac{DY}{(L-U)^2} \le 0.03$$

## C-5. LENGTH OF LEG REQUIRED

### Two-Member System, Both Ends Fixed, Thermal Expansion in Plane of Members

![C-5. Length of Leg Required — Two-Member System, Both Ends Fixed, Thermal Expansion in Plane of Members. Nomograph plotting $LS_A/10^4 e$ versus K with nominal pipe size curves \(1", 1½", 2", 2½", 3", 4", 5", 6", 8", 10", 12", 14", 16", 18", 20", 24", 30", 36"\). Accompanying sketch shows two-member system ABC with leg L from A to B and leg KL from B to C.](figures/MWK_1956_p0345_fig01_c-5-length-of-leg-required-two-member-sy.png)

$L$ = Length of leg $AB$, ft.

$e$ = Unit linear thermal expansion, in./ft.

Value of $E$ used = $29 \times 10^6$ psi.

$S_A$ = Code allowable stress range $(1.25S_c + 0.25S_h)$, psi.

Multiply $L$ by $K$ to obtain length of leg $BC$ required.

---

## C-6. MOMENTS AND FORCES

### Two-Member System, Both Ends Fixed

### Thermal Expansion in Plane of Members

![C-6. Moments and Forces — Two-Member System, Both Ends Fixed, Thermal Expansion in Plane of Members. Log-log chart of $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ versus $K$ \(ranging from 0.1 to 1.0\), with diagram inserts for $K<1$ and $K>1$ configurations and an axis-convention sketch showing $F_x$, $F_y$, and $M_z$ at the corner.](figures/MWK_1956_p0346_fig01_c-6-moments-and-forces-two-member-system.png)

For $K < 1$:

$$F_{xA} = -F_{xC} = -10^4 A_1 I e / L^2$$
$$F_{yA} = -F_{yC} = +10^4 A_2 I e / L^2$$
$$M_{xA} = +10^4 A_3 I e / L$$
$$M_{xC} = -10^4 A_4 I e / L$$

For $K > 1$:

$$F_{xA} = -F_{xC} = -10^4 A_1 I e / (KL)^2$$
$$F_{yA} = -F_{yC} = +10^4 A_2 I e / (KL)^2$$
$$M_{xA} = 10^4 A_3 I e / KL$$
$$M_{xC} = -10^4 A_4 I e / KL$$

$F$ = Force, lb.
$M$ = Moment, ft-lb.

First subscript denotes *direction*.

Second subscript denotes *location*.

Signs are those of forces or *moments acting on anchors*.

$I$ = Moment of inertia of pipe, in.$^4$.
$e$ = Unit linear thermal expansion, in./ft.
Value of $E$ used = $29 \times 10^6$ psi.

![C-7. Length of Leg Required - Two-Member System, Both Ends Fixed - One Support Displaced in the Direction of the Adjoining Member. Inset diagram shows two-member system ABC with leg AB of length L, displacement $\\Delta$ at end A, and KL representing length of BC.](figures/MWK_1956_p0347_fig01_c-7-length-of-leg-required-two-member-sy.png)

Multiply $L$ by $K$ to obtain length of $BC$ required.

Chart of $\\bar{A}_1$, $\\bar{A}_2$, $\\bar{A}_3$, $\\bar{A}_4$, $\\bar{A}_5$ versus $K$ for $0 \\leq K \\leq 1.0$, with accompanying schematic of the two-member system showing supports A, B, C, dimensions L, $K L$, and displacement $\\Delta$, plus a moment-diagram sketch.](figures/MWK_1956_p0350_fig01_c-10-moments-and-forces-two-member-syste.png)

Value of $E$ used = $29 \times 10^6$ psi.

## C-11. REQUIRED HEIGHT

### Symmetrical Expansion Loop

![C-11. Required Height - Symmetrical Expansion Loop. Chart plotting $\\frac{L^2 S_A}{10^7 D \\Delta}$ versus $K_2$ with curves for various $K_1$ values.](figures/MWK_1956_p0351_fig01_c-11-required-height-symmetrical-expansi.png)

$L$ = Length from $A$ to $B$, ft.

$L_o = \frac{1}{2}L(1 - K_1)$

$\Delta$ = Expansion from $A'$ to $B'$, in.

$D$ = Outside diameter of pipe, in.

Value of $E$ used = $29 \times 10^6$ psi.

$S_A$ = Code allowable stress range $(1.25 S_c + 0.25 S_h)$, psi.

Multiply $L_o$ by $K_1$ and $K_2$ to obtain dimensions of loop.

![C-16. Span vs. Stress, Horizontal Pipe Lines, Uniform Load](figures/MWK_1956_p0357_fig01_c-16-span-vs-stress-horizontal-pipe-line.png)

Formula: $S = 1.2wl^2/Z$

Key:
1. Connect $Z$ with $w$ locating turning point ($A$).
2. Connect ($A$) with $s$ locating $l$.
   Connect ($A$) with $l$ locating $s$.

## C-17. Span vs. Natural Frequency and vs. Deflection

### Horizontal Pipe Lines, Uniform Load

![C-17. Span vs. Natural Frequency and vs. Deflection - Horizontal Pipe Lines, Uniform Load. Nomograph with axes: I = Moment of Inertia \(IN.4\), l = Pipe Span \(FT\), f_n = Approximate Natural Frequency \(cycles per sec\), δ = Deflection \(IN.\), E = Modulus of Elasticity \(LB PER SQ IN\), T = Temperature \(F\), w = Total Unit Weight \(LB PER FT\).](figures/MWK_1956_p0358_fig01_c-17-span-vs-natural-frequency-and-vs-de.png)

Formulas: $\delta = 17.1 w l^4 / EI$  $f_n = 3.13/\sqrt{\delta}$

Key:
1. Connect $E$ (or $T$) with $I$ locating turning point ($A$) at intersection on $l$.
2. Connect ($A$) with $w$ locating turning point ($B$) at intersection on $I$.
3. Connect ($B$) with $l$ locating $\delta$ (or $l$).
   Connect ($B$) with $\delta$ (or $f_n$) locating $l$.

Example: Given: $E = 29 \times 10^6$ psi, $I = 2840$ in.$^4$, $w = 320$ lb/ft.
Result: $f_n = 0.76$ cy/sec, $\delta = 0.17$ in.

## 5A-1 Introduction

THE Kellogg general analytical method for relating the expansion displacements of space piping systems to terminal and intermediate forces, moments, and stresses was organized for internal company use in the early 1930's, was formally published in 1941 in the First Edition of the "Design of Piping Systems." In the Second Edition of the "Design of Piping Systems," published in 1956, the presentation was extended to include the combined effects of terminal and intermediate restraints, and of concentrated and distributed loads. This Second Edition also provided the mathematical basis for the simplification of complex problems by the inversion method, and a brief discussion of the then current application of computing machines.

In recent years, rapid developments in the field of digital computers have permitted the solution of increasingly complex piping systems with economy and versatility, not previously attainable. Although exploratory computer solutions were carried out much earlier, routine solutions were first obtained by Kellogg in 1954 using card programmed computing equipment. The magnetic drum type computer obtained in 1956 reduced computation time to one-tenth. The magnetic core type computer acquired by Kellogg in 1961 has further reduced computation time by still another factor of ten. With speed of this order, the ultimate objective of completely automatic machine analysis of arbitrarily complex piping systems has become a reality.

With the development of computer programs of ever widening scope, the task of the program planner has become more demanding. The program must be so planned that any conceivable configuration can be analyzed, regardless of the number of branches, anchors, stops, or internal multiple closed loops. The program should require a minimum amount of input data and provide a maximum amount of automation. Essential to the attainment of these objectives is a rigorous statement of the computational problem in concise mathematical terms. The importance of this is attested by the growing acceptance of the notation of matrix algebra in the description of the piping problem. In recent years, Kellogg engineers and mathematicians have used vector and matrix algebra in re-deriving the shape coefficients for spatial pipes of any orientation and securing efficient solutions to piping problems of any complexity. This chapter summarizes the current Kellogg approach.

In Section 5A-2, the symbols and nomenclature will be defined, followed by a step-by-step derivation of the shape coefficient matrix, referred to an arbitrary set of right-hand orthogonal coordinate axes. It will be shown that the shape coefficient matrix can be expressed as a function of two submatrices, one of which refers only to a local origin and a local coordinate system and, hence, is independent of the skewness of the member with respect to the common coordinate system chosen for the entire piping system. The other matrix serves to transfer the local coordinates to the common coordinate system, and is independent of the geometrical configuration of the pipe element, whether it be straight or curved. Following the theoretical derivation, the shape coefficient matrices for straight pipes and circular bends will be constructed, and a method of obtaining these matrices from minimal input data will be given.

---

In Section 5A-3, the two anchor problems will be extended to the multiple branch and loop problems in a manner that provides convenient automatic assembly of shape coefficient matrices by computer. Systems with intermediate restraints will be treated, including skew stops. A brief discussion on computer solutions currently in use will be presented in Section 5A-4, with the machine input data and printout results for a simple illustrative problem. Finally, the chapter will be concluded with a brief review of a selected bibliography.

## 5A-2 Derivation of the Shape Coefficient Matrix

**1. Definitions and Nomenclature.** Unless otherwise specified in the text, the following definitions and nomenclature will be used consistently in this chapter.

(i) A vector is distinguished from a scalar by a bar over the symbol, thus $\bar{f}$ is a vector; $f_i$ is a scalar representing the component of $\bar{f}$ in the $i$-direction.

A vector with a superscript, $\bar{F}^i$, represents a six-component force (including moment) vector acting on the pipe branch $i$. Also, $\bar{x}^i$ represents a six-component displacement (including rotation) vector at the end of branch $i$.

(ii) An element in a matrix, located at the $i$-th row and the $j$-th column, is represented by a symbol with two subscripts, such as $A_{ij}$.

A matrix consisting of an array of numbers, $A_{ij}$, is represented by $|A_{ij}|$, or by a capital letter without subscript and vertical bars, e.g., $A$, $B$, etc.

A matrix with a superscript, $A^i$, represents the shape coefficient matrix of the branch $i$.

The transpose of a matrix $A$ (or $|A_{ij}|$) is denoted by $A'$ (or $|A_{ji}|$).

A zero (null) matrix is denoted as $|0|$. A diagonal unit matrix is denoted as $|I|$.

(iii) $\sum\limits_{i} = \sum\limits_{i=1, 2, 3}$ represents a summation with respect to $i$ of the term or terms following this sign, when $i$ varies from 1 to 3.

(iv) A right-hand, orthogonal coordinate system is denoted by one symbol with permutable subscripts 1, 2 and 3. The following coordinate systems are defined:

a. At the chosen origin, $O'$: $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, $\bar{x}_3$, called the $x$-system;

b. At the convenient local origin, $q$: $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, $\bar{x}_3$, called the $x_q$-system;

c. At any point along the pipe line, $P$: $\bar{\xi}_1$, $\bar{\xi}_2$, $\bar{\xi}_3$, called the $\xi$-system.

Note that $\bar{x}_i$, $\bar{x}_i$ and $\bar{\xi}_i$ are all unit vectors.

(v) The following position vectors are defined:

a. With respect to the $x$-system, the position vector of point $q$ is:

$$\bar{q}(x) = \sum_{i} q_i \bar{x}_i$$

and the position vector of point $P$ is:

$$\bar{p} = \sum_{i} x_i \bar{x}_i$$

b. With respect to the $x_q$-system, the position vector of point $P$ is:

$$\bar{p} = \sum_{i} \rho_i \bar{x}_i$$

Figure 5A.1 shows a space curve in the $x$-system. Any point $P$ on the curve can be defined by the equation:

$$\bar{p} = \sum_{i} p_i \bar{x}_i = \bar{q} + \bar{p} = \bar{q} + \sum_{i} \rho_i \bar{x}_i \quad (5A.1)$$

(vi) A vector defined in one coordinate system may be transformed to another system through a linear transformation defined as follows:

a. From the $\lambda$-system to the $\xi$-system:

$$\bar{\xi}_j = \sum_{i} \xi_{ji} \bar{x}_i \qquad j = 1, 2, 3 \quad (5A.2)$$

b. From the $x$-system to the $\lambda$-system:

$$\bar{x}_j = \sum_{i} \lambda_{ji} \bar{x}_i \qquad j = 1, 2, 3 \quad (5A.3)$$

It may be noted that $\xi_{ji}$ represent direction cosines of the unit vector $\bar{\xi}_j$ with respect to

(vii) *Nomenclature*

$\bar{F}$ = Redundant Force Vector
$\bar{M}$ = Redundant Moment Vector
$\bar{\Delta}$ = Displacement Vector
$\bar{\Phi}$ = Rotation Vector
$\bar{f}$ = Internal Force Vector

$F_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{F}$ in $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, and $\bar{x}_3$ direction, respectively.

$M_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{M}$ in $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, and $\bar{x}_3$ direction, respectively.

$\Delta_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{\Delta}$ in $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, and $\bar{x}_3$ direction, respectively.

$\phi_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{\Phi}$ in $\bar{x}_1$, $\bar{x}_2$, and $\bar{x}_3$ direction, respectively.

$f_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{f}$ in $\bar{\xi}_1$, $\bar{\xi}_2$, and $\bar{\xi}_3$ direction, respectively.

$m_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Components of $\bar{m}$ in $\bar{\xi}_1$, $\bar{\xi}_2$, and $\bar{\xi}_3$ direction, respectively.

$a_{ij}$, $b_{i(i=1,2,3)}$ = Flexibility factors as defined in Eq. 5A.9.

$\alpha_{ij}$, $\beta_{ij}$ = As defined in Eqs. 5A.14 and 5A.24

$\bar{x}_r = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_2$, as defined in Eq. 5A.22
$\psi_1 = \theta + \sin \theta$

$k_2$ = Out-of-plane Bending Factor of a Pipe
