## 2. The Shape Coefficient Matrix.

In piping analyses, it is convenient to consider a complex piping system, consisting of straight and curved members randomly oriented in space to be a cantilever (or a series of cantilevers), rigidly fixed at one end and free at the other (or others) upon which the redundant forces $\bar{F}$ and moments $\bar{M}$ act to preserve the prescribed physical conditions. These redundant forces and moments and the corresponding displacements are functions of the coordinates of the points of application. To facilitate analyses, it is customary to consider all the redundant forces and moments, and the corresponding displacements, to occur at a common origin and in the fixed $x$-system.

In what follows, we shall develop the shape coefficient matrix for a two-anchor system subject to thermal expansion. The generalization of this development to multiple anchor and loop problems will be discussed in Sec. 5A.3. We define:

$$\bar{F} = \sum_i F_i \bar{x}_i$$
$$\bar{M} = \sum_i M_i \bar{x}_i \tag{5A.4}$$

as the redundant forces and moments at the free end of the cantilever, but transferred to the common origin; also, the corresponding translative and rotational displacements at the same origin as:

$$\bar{\Delta} = \sum_i \Delta_i \bar{x}_i$$
$$\bar{\Phi} = \sum_i \phi_i \bar{x}_i \tag{5A.5}$$

The condition of static equilibrium requires that the internal forces and moments at any point along the line be:

$$\begin{cases} \bar{f} = \sum_i f_i \bar{\xi}_i = \bar{F}, \\ \bar{m} = \sum_i m_i \bar{\xi}_i = \bar{M} - \bar{p} \times \bar{F}. \end{cases} \tag{5A.6}$$

The force and moment components may be obtained by vector algebra as follows:

$$\begin{cases} f_i = \bar{\xi}_i \cdot \bar{F}, \\ m_i = \bar{\xi}_i \cdot \bar{M} - \bar{\xi}_i \cdot \bar{p} \times \bar{F} = \bar{\xi}_i \cdot \bar{M} + \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_i \cdot \bar{F}. \end{cases} \tag{5A.7}$$

The total internal strain energy (a scalar quantity), induced by $\bar{F}$ and $\bar{M}$ in the pipe is:

$$U = \frac{1}{2EI} \int_s \sum_i (a_i f_i^2 + b_i m_i^2) \, ds, \tag{5A.8}$$

where $a_i$ are the flexibility factors associated with the so-called direct effects (axial and transverse shear) and $b_i$, those associated with bending (including torsion) effects. Taking Poisson's ratio as 0.3, and assuming thin pipe of uniform stiffness $EI$, the quantities $a_i$ and $b_i$ have the following values:

$$\begin{aligned} a_1 &= 0.5\, r^2 & b_1 &= 1.3 \\ a_2 &= 2.6\, r^2 & b_2 &= k_2 \\ a_3 &= 2.6\, r^2 & b_3 &= k_1 \end{aligned} \tag{5A.9}$$

---

where $r$ is the mean radius of the pipe, $k_1$ and $k_2$ are the in-plane and out-of-plane bending factors. If there is any portion of the pipe with stiffness $E I_s X$ different from the constant $EI$, the integration of Eq. 5A.8 must be performed in segments, and a correction factor $Q = EI/E_sI_s$ be applied to all $a_i$ and $b_i$.

Using Castigliano's Theorem which states that:

$$\begin{cases} \phi_j = \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial M_j}, \\ \Delta_j = \dfrac{\partial U}{\partial F_j}, \end{cases} \quad j = 1, 2, 3 \tag{5A.10}$$

we obtain from Eqs. 5A.7 and 5A.8 the following equations:

$$\begin{cases} EI\phi_j = \displaystyle\int \sum_i b_i m_i \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial M_j} ds \\ \qquad = \displaystyle\int \sum_i b_i [\xi_i \cdot (\overline{M} - \overline{\rho} \times \overline{F})] \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial M_j} ds, \\ \\ EI\Delta_j = \displaystyle\int \sum_i \left( a_i f_i \dfrac{\partial f_i}{\partial F_j} + b_i m_i \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial F_j} \right) ds \\ \qquad = \displaystyle\int \sum_i \xi_i \cdot \left[ a_i \overline{F} \dfrac{\partial f_i}{\partial F_j} \right. \\ \qquad \left. + b_i (\overline{M} - \overline{\rho} \times \overline{F}) \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial F_j} \right] ds, \\ \qquad j = 1, 2, 3, \end{cases} \tag{5A.11}$$

From Eqs. 5A.4 and 5A.7, we see that:

$$\begin{cases} \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial M_j} = -\xi_i \cdot \overline{z}_j = \dfrac{\partial f_i}{\partial F_j}, \\ \dfrac{\partial m_i}{\partial F_j} = -\xi_i \cdot (\overline{\rho} \times \overline{z}_j) = (\overline{\rho} \times \xi_i) \cdot \overline{z}_j. \end{cases} \tag{5A.12}$$

Substituting Eq. 5A.12 in Eq. 5A.11 and collecting terms, we get:

$$\begin{cases} EI\phi_j = \displaystyle\sum_k M_k \int \sum_i b_i \alpha_{ik} \alpha_{ik} ds \\ \qquad + \displaystyle\sum_k F_k \int \sum_i b_i \beta_{ik} \beta_{ij} ds, \\ \\ EI\Delta_j = \displaystyle\sum_k M_k \int \sum_i b_i \beta_{ij} \alpha_{ik} ds \\ \qquad + \displaystyle\sum_k F_k \int \sum_i (a_i \alpha_{ik} \alpha_{ij} + b_i \beta_{ik} \beta_{ij}) ds, \\ \qquad j = 1, 2, 3, \end{cases} \tag{5A.13}$$

where

$$\begin{cases} \alpha_{ij} = \xi_i \cdot \overline{z}_j, \\ \beta_{ij} = (\overline{\rho} \times \xi_i) \cdot \overline{z}_j. \end{cases} \tag{5A.14}$$

We introduce the notation:

$$\begin{cases} W_{jk} = \displaystyle\int \sum_i b_i \alpha_{ij} \alpha_{ik} ds, \\ U_{jk} = \displaystyle\int \sum_i (a_i \alpha_{ij} \alpha_{ik} + b_i \beta_{ij} \beta_{ik}) ds, \\ V_{jk} = \displaystyle\int \sum_i b_i \beta_{ij} \alpha_{ik} ds. \end{cases} \tag{5A.15}$$

It may be noted in Eq. 5A.15 that the subscripts $j$ and $k$ can be interchanged for $W_{jk}$ and $U_{jk}$ without affecting the results, but this is not true for $V_{jk}$. In other words, the matrices $|W_{jk}|$, $|U_{jk}|$ are symmetric but $|V_{jk}|$ is not. Thus we have:

$$\begin{cases} W_{jk} = W_{kj}, \quad \text{or} \quad W = W', \\ U_{jk} = U_{kj}, \quad \text{or} \quad U = U', \\ V_{kj} = V'_{jk} = \displaystyle\int \sum_i b_i \beta_{ik} \alpha_{ij} ds. \end{cases} \tag{5A.16}$$

Substituting Eqs. 5A.15 and 5A.16 in Eq. 5A.13, we get:

$$\begin{cases} EI\phi_j = \displaystyle\sum_k M_k W_{jk} + \sum_k F_k V_{jk}, \\ EI\Delta_j = \displaystyle\sum_k M_k V'_{jk} + \sum_k F_k U_{jk}, \end{cases} \quad j = 1, 2, 3$$

or in a detailed form:

$$\begin{cases} EI\phi_1 = W_{11}M_1 + W_{12}M_2 + W_{13}M_3 + V_{11}F_1 \\ \qquad + V_{12}F_2 + V_{13}F_3, \\ EI\phi_2 = W_{21}M_1 + W_{22}M_2 + W_{23}M_3 + V_{21}F_1 \\ \qquad + V_{22}F_2 + V_{23}F_3, \\ EI\phi_3 = W_{31}M_1 + W_{32}M_2 + W_{33}M_3 + V_{31}F_1 \\ \qquad + V_{32}F_2 + V_{33}F_3, \\ EI\Delta_1 = V_{11}M_1 + V_{21}M_2 + V_{31}M_3 + U_{11}F_1 \\ \qquad + U_{12}F_2 + U_{13}F_3, \\ EI\Delta_2 = V_{12}M_1 + V_{22}M_2 + V_{32}M_3 + U_{21}F_1 \\ \qquad + U_{22}F_2 + U_{23}F_3, \\ EI\Delta_3 = V_{13}M_1 + V_{23}M_2 + V_{33}M_3 + U_{31}F_1 \\ \qquad + U_{32}F_2 + U_{33}F_3. \end{cases} \tag{5A.17}$$

Equation 5A.17 can be written simply in the matrix form:

$$EI \begin{vmatrix} \phi_j \\ \Delta_j \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} W_{jk} & V_{jk} \\ V'_{jk} & U_{jk} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} M_k \\ F_k \end{vmatrix} = A \begin{vmatrix} M_k \\ F_k \end{vmatrix}, \tag{5A.18}$$

---

A MATRIX METHOD OF PIPING ANALYSIS AND USE OF DIGITAL COMPUTERS 365

where the displacement and force (including moment) matrices are column matrices, while matrix $A$ is a $6 \times 6$ square matrix known under various names as shape coefficient, influence coefficient, or performance, matrix. According to Maxwell's law of reciprocity, matrix $A$ should be, and is, in the present case, symmetrical about the diagonal.

It should be noted that the elements in matrix $A$ are obtained by performing line integrations in Eq. 5A.15. Since a line integral can be evaluated by segments, i.e., a line integral is the sum of line integrals of the component segments, the shape coefficient matrix for the entire pipe may be obtained by summing the shape coefficient matrices of the component segments.

Equation 5A.18 can be used to solve the redundant moments and forces at the freed anchor provided that the displacements at this anchor are prescribed. Once the redundants become known, Eq. 5A.7 will give the internal forces at any point along the pipe as follows:

$$
\left|\begin{array}{c} m_l \\ f_l \end{array}\right| = \left|\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_{lj} & \beta_{lj} \\ 0 & \alpha_{lj} \end{array}\right| \left|\begin{array}{c} M_j \\ F_j \end{array}\right|. \quad (5A.19)
$$

The elements $\alpha_{lj}$, and $\beta_{lj}$ are determined by Eq. 5A.14.

## 3. The Submatrices of the Shape Coefficient Matrix.

The coefficients $\alpha_{ij}$ and $\beta_{ij}$, being function of direction cosines and the position vector $\bar{p}$, may be easily obtained for favorably oriented straight line pipes or simple bends. If the pipe is skewed with respect to the fixed $x$-system, we shall select a convenient local origin, $\bar{q}$, as shown in Figure 5A.1, Section 3A-2.1, and introduce a local coordinate system with respect to which the given segment of pipe will have the simplest form of shape coefficient matrix. We can then refer the shape coefficient matrix back to the $x$-system by means of suitable matrix operations which will be derived below.

Let the local coordinate system be identified as the $\xi$-system. Using Eqs. 5A.1 and 5A.2, one gets:

$$
\bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_i = \bar{q} \times \sum_k \xi_{ki}\bar{x}_i + \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_i. \quad (5A.20)
$$

Introducing the vector $\bar{u}_r$ defined in the $x$-system as:

$$
\bar{u}_r = \bar{q} \times \bar{x}_r = \sum_k u_{rk}\bar{x}_k, \quad (5A.21)
$$

and the vector $\bar{e}_r$ defined in the $\xi$-system as:

$$
\bar{e}_r = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_r = \sum_k e_{rk}\bar{\lambda}_k, \quad (5A.22)
$$

Equation 5A.20 may be written as:

$$
\bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_i = \sum_r \xi_{ri}\bar{u}_r + \sum_r e_{ri}\bar{\lambda}_r \quad (5A.23)
$$
$$
= \sum_r \xi_{ri} \sum_k u_{rk}\bar{x}_k + \sum_r e_{ri} \sum_k \lambda_{rk}\bar{x}_k.
$$

Substituting Eqs. 5A.2, 5A.3 and 5A.23 in Eq. 5A.14, we get:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l} \alpha_{ij} = \sum_r \xi_{ri}\lambda_{rj} \\ \beta_{ij} = \sum_r \xi_{ri}u_{rj} + \sum_r e_{ri}\lambda_{rj}. \end{array}\right. \quad (5A.24)
$$

Equation 5A.15 will then take the following form:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l} W_{jk} = \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i \lambda_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}\xi_{li} \, ds \\ U_{jk} = \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i \lambda_{sk} \sum_i a_i \int \xi_{li}\xi_{li} \, ds \\ \quad + \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i u_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int e_{li}e_{li} \, ds \\ \quad + \sum_s u_{sj} \sum_i \lambda_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}e_{li} \, ds \\ \quad + \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i u_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}e_{li} \, ds \\ \quad + \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i u_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int e_{li}e_{li} \, ds, \\ V_{jk} = \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i \lambda_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}\xi_{li} \, ds \\ \quad + \sum_s \lambda_{sj} \sum_i \lambda_{sk} \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}e_{li} \, ds. \end{array}\right. \quad (5A.25)
$$

We define:

$$
L = |\lambda_{kj}|, N = |u_{kj}|,
$$
$$
B = |B_{ri}| = \left| \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}\xi_{li} \, ds \right|, \quad (5A.26)
$$
$$
C = |C_{ri}| = \left| \sum_i a_i \int \xi_{li}\xi_{li} \, ds + \sum_i b_i \int e_{li}e_{li} \, ds \right|,
$$
$$
D = |D_{ri}| = \left| \sum_i b_i \int \xi_{li}e_{li} \, ds \right|,
$$

each being a $3 \times 3$ matrix. Upon substitution of Eq. 5A.26 in the matrices of Eq. 5A.25, we get:

$$
|W_{jk}| = L'BL,
$$
$$
|U_{jk}| = L'CL + N'BN + N'DL + L'D'N, \quad (5A.27)
$$
$$
|V_{jk}| = L'BN + L'DL.
$$

---

Substituting Eq. 5A.27 in matrix $A$ which is defined in Eq. 5A.18, it is easy to verify that:

$$A = \begin{vmatrix} L' & O \\ N' & L' \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} B & D \\ D' & C \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} L & N \\ O & L \end{vmatrix} \quad (5A.28)$$

where $O$ represents a $3 \times 3$ null matrix. If we let:

$$X = \begin{vmatrix} B & D \\ D' & C \end{vmatrix}$$

$$Y = \begin{vmatrix} L & N \\ O & L \end{vmatrix} \quad (5A.29)$$

be the submatrices of the matrix $A$, Eq. 5A.28 can then be written as:

$$A = Y'XY \quad (5A.30)$$

The following observations may be made on the submatrices in Eq. 5A.30:

1. The $3 \times 3$ matrices $B$, $C$, and $D$ (Eq. 5A.26) in $X$ matrix have identical meanings in the $\lambda$-system as $|W_{ij}|$, $|U_{jl}|$ and $|V_{il}|$ (Eq. 5A.13) in the $x$-system. In fact, if the local origin is taken as the common origin, and the $\lambda$-system identical to the $x$-system, $N$ would become a null matrix as can be seen from Eqs. 5A.21 and 5A.26, and $L$ would become a diagonal unit matrix as can be seen from Eqs. 5A.3 and 5A.26. Consequently, $A$ simply becomes $X$. Therefore, $X$ may be called the shape coefficient matrix, but referred to the $\lambda$-system. It is implicit here that $X$ can be computed for every segment of a pipe irrespective of the $x$-system.

2. The $\lambda$-system, or the coordinates at the local origin, can be chosen so as to make the construction of the $X$ matrix as simple as possible. The correct choice of the $\lambda$-system for common piping configurations is not difficult to obtain as will be demonstrated in the illustrative examples in Section 5A-2.4.

3. The $Y$ matrix, consisting of terms which are functions of the position vector $\bar{q}$ and the local coordinate $\bar{\lambda}_i$ only, can be computed for every piping segment irrespective of its geometrical configuration. Once $\bar{q}$ and $\bar{\lambda}_i$ are given in the $x$-system, $Y$ follows from Eq. 5A.29.

When matrix $A$ becomes available for every segment of the pipe, the shape coefficient matrix for the entire pipe may be obtained by summation. Equation 5A.18 can again be used to obtain the redundants and Eq. 5A.19 the internal forces at any point along the pipe, except that $\alpha_{ij}$, $\beta_{ij}$ are now defined by Eq. 5A.24.

## 4. Illustrative Examples

**a. Straight pipe (Figure 5A.2).** A straight pipe is chosen at the mid-point. The $\lambda$-system and $\bar{\xi}$-system are defined as shown. The systems are chosen such that each axis will coincide with the proper principal axis of the pipe.

Let the length $q\bar{p}$ be denoted as $s$. With respect to the $\lambda$-system, the following vectors with components in the 1, 2, and 3 directions listed in parentheses are first determined:

$$\bar{p} \quad (s, \; 0, \; 0)$$

$$\bar{\xi}_1 \quad (1, \; 0, \; 0)$$

$$\bar{\xi}_2 \quad (0, \; 1, \; 0)$$

$$\bar{\xi}_3 \quad (0, \; 0, \; 1)$$

$$\bar{e}_1 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_1 \quad (0, \; 0, \; 0)$$

$$\bar{e}_2 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_2 \quad (0, \; 0, \; s)$$

$$\bar{e}_3 = \bar{p} \times \bar{\xi}_3 \quad (0, \; -s, \; 0)$$

Then, following Eq. 5A.26, the submatrices $B$ and $D$ can be computed as follows:

$$B = |B_{rt}| = \sum_i b_i \int_{-l/2}^{l/2} \bar{\xi}_{ri} \bar{\xi}_{ti} \, ds$$

$$= \int_{-l/2}^{l/2} \sum_i b_i \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} ds$$

$$= \begin{vmatrix} b_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b_2 l & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_3 l \end{vmatrix}$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= \left| \sum_i a_i \int \xi_{i\epsilon} \xi_{i1} \, ds + \sum_i b_i \int \epsilon_{i\epsilon} \epsilon_{i1} \, ds \right| \\
&= \left| \begin{matrix} a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a_2 l & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a_3 l \end{matrix} \right| + \left| \begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12} \end{matrix} \right| \\
&= \left| \begin{matrix} a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a_2 l + \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a_3 l + \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12} \end{matrix} \right|
\end{aligned}
$$

$D = |0|.$

The matrix $X$ takes the following form:

$$
X = \left| \begin{matrix}
b_1 l & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & b_2 l & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & b_3 l & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & a_1 l & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & a_2 l + \dfrac{b_2 l^3}{12} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & a_3 l + \dfrac{b_3 l^3}{12}
\end{matrix} \right|
$$

b. *Circular Bend* (Figure 5A.3). The $\lambda$ and $\bar{\xi}$-systems are chosen as shown, $\bar{\lambda}_3$ being parallel to the chord of the circular arc and $\bar{\lambda}_2$ directed toward the center of the bend, $Q$; whereas $\bar{\xi}_1$ is tangent to the arc in the increasing direction of the arc length and $\bar{\xi}_3$ is directed toward point $q$.

![Figure 5A.3](figures/MWK_1956_p0368_fig01_figure-5a-3.png)

Let the arc length $QP$ be denoted as $s$. Then the following vectors can be specified in the $\lambda$-system:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{p} &\left( R \sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad R \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\
\bar{\xi}_1 &\left( \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad -\sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\
\bar{\xi}_2 &\left( -\sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad -\cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right), \\
\bar{\xi}_3 &(0, \quad 0, \quad -1).
\end{aligned}
$$

It follows that:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{e}_1 &\left( 0, \quad 0, \quad -R \right), \\
\bar{e}_2 &\left( 0, \quad 0, \quad 0 \right), \\
\bar{e}_3 &\left( -R \cos \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad R \sin \dfrac{s}{R}, \quad 0 \right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Equation 5A.26 gives:

$$
B = \int_{-\frac{R\theta}{2}}^{\frac{R\theta}{2}} \left| \begin{matrix} \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & -\sin \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ -\sin \dfrac{s}{R} & -\cos \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{matrix} \right| \cdot \left| \begin{matrix} b_1 \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & -b_1 \sin \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ -b_2 \sin \dfrac{s}{R} & b_2 \cos \dfrac{s}{R} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -b_3 \end{matrix} \right| ds
$$

$$
= \left| \begin{matrix} \dfrac{R}{2} (b_1 \psi_1 + b_2 \psi_2) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{R}{2} (b_1 \psi_2 + b_2 \psi_1) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_3 R \theta \end{matrix} \right|
$$

where

$$
\psi_1 = \theta + \sin \theta, \qquad \psi_2 = \theta - \sin \theta. \tag{a}
$$

---

Similarly,

$$C = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{R}{2}(a_1\psi_1 + a_2\psi_2 + b_3R^2\psi_1) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{R}{2}(a_1\psi_2 + a_2\varphi_1 + b_3R^2\psi_2) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & R\theta(a_2 + b_1R^2) \end{vmatrix}$$

$$D = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & -2b_1R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2b_2R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix}$$

Then the $X$ matrix is:

$$X = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{R}{2}(b_1\varphi_1 + b_3\varphi_2) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -2b_1R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} \\ 0 & \dfrac{R}{2}(b_1\varphi_2 + b_3\varphi_1) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & b_2R\theta & 2b_2R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2b_2R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} & \dfrac{R}{2}(a_1\varphi_1 + a_2\varphi_2 + b_3R^2\varphi_1) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dfrac{R}{2}(a_1\varphi_2 + a_2\varphi_1 + b_3R^2\varphi_2) & 0 \\ -2b_1R^2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & R\theta(a_2 + b_1R^2) \end{vmatrix}$$

c. *Construction of the $Y$ Matrix from Working Points.* So far, only the $X$ matrix has been constructed for a straight pipe as well as for a circular bend. To refer the shape coefficient matrix to a definite $z$-system at the chosen origin $O'$, the $X$ matrix appearing in Eq. 5A.30 must also be constructed, and the proper shape coefficient matrix will simply be $Y'XY$.

It is customary to specify working points whose coordinates are given in the $z$-system. For a straight pipe, the starting and terminal points are usually given (Figure 5A.4), and the necessary calculation for the construction of $Y$ matrix can be outlined below.

Given

$$\vec{a} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}_z$$

then

$$\left.\begin{aligned} l &= \sqrt{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}}, \\ \bar{x}_1 &= \vec{a}/l, \\ \bar{x}_2 &= \text{any unit vector satisfying } \bar{x}_1 \cdot \bar{x}_2 = 0, \\ \bar{x}_3 &= \bar{x}_1 \times \bar{x}_2, \end{aligned}\right\} \quad (b)$$

and, finally,

$$\bar{q} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{a} + \bar{b}). \tag{c}$$

Now, let $\bar{q}$ be expressed by:

$$\bar{q} = q_1\bar{z}_1 + q_2\bar{z}_2 + q_3\bar{z}_3$$

![Figure 5A.4](figures/MWK_1956_p0369_fig01_figure-5a-4.png)

---

A MATRIX METHOD OF PIPING ANALYSIS AND USE OF DIGITAL COMPUTERS    369

![Figure 5A.5](figures/MWK_1956_p0370_fig01_figure-5a-5.png)

we have

$$\bar{k}_1 = \frac{\bar{l} + \bar{l}'}{2 \cos \frac{\phi}{2}},$$

and

$$\bar{k}_2 = \frac{\bar{l}' \times \bar{i}}{\sin \theta}, \quad \text{(f)}$$

$$\bar{k}_3 = \bar{k}_2 \times \bar{k}_1.$$

Substituting $\bar{\phi}$ in Eq. 5A.21, with Eq. 5A.3, we get:

$$\begin{aligned} u_{r1} &= q_3\lambda_{x9} - q_2\lambda_{x2} \\ u_{r2} &= q_3\lambda_{r1} - q_1\lambda_{r3} \\ u_{r3} &= q_1\lambda_{r2} - q_2\lambda_{r1} \end{aligned} \quad r = 1, 2, 3 \quad \text{(d)}$$

where $\lambda_{x2}$, for instance, is the direction cosine of $\bar{\lambda}_x$ with respect to $\bar{x}_2$, etc. All the direction cosines are available from Eq. (b). The $Y$ matrix can finally be written as:

[TABLE: Y matrix expression (e)]

$$Y = \begin{vmatrix} \lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \lambda_{13} & u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ \lambda_{21} & \lambda_{22} & \lambda_{23} & u_{21} & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ \lambda_{31} & \lambda_{32} & \lambda_{33} & u_{31} & u_{32} & u_{33} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \lambda_{13} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \lambda_{21} & \lambda_{22} & \lambda_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \lambda_{31} & \lambda_{32} & \lambda_{33} \end{vmatrix} \quad \text{(e)}$$

For a circular bend, three working points (a, b, and c in Figure 5A.5) are usually given in addition to the radius of the bend, $R$. Let,

$$\bar{d} = \bar{a} - \bar{c}$$

$$\bar{d}' = \bar{b} - \bar{c}.$$

Then the lengths $ac$ and $cb$ are respectively,

$$l = \sqrt{\bar{d} \cdot \bar{d}}, \qquad l' = \sqrt{\bar{d}' \cdot \bar{d}'},$$

and the unit vectors are

$$\bar{i} = \bar{d}/l, \qquad \bar{i}' = \bar{d}'/l'.$$

Since

$$\bar{i} \cdot \bar{i}' = \cos \theta,$$

The position vector $\bar{q}$ can be expressed as:

$$\bar{q} = \bar{c} - \frac{R}{\cos \frac{\phi}{2}} \quad \text{(g)}$$

It is clear that the matrix $Y$ for the bend can be constructed by an identical procedure as outlined previously for a straight pipe.

## 5A-3   A Matrix Method of Piping Analysis

The shape coefficient matrix derived on the basis of a two-anchor problem was presented in the previous section. In order to solve a more complex piping system, a certain generalization will be necessary. To illustrate this, we shall consider a system with two anchors and four closed loops as shown in Figure 5A.6. Subsequently, the effect of intermediate restraints will be discussed.

![Figure 5A.6](figures/MWK_1956_p0370_fig02_figure-5a-6.png)

---

### 1. Systems with Multiple Anchors and Loops.

Denote the fixed anchor as point $0'$, and label all the joints sequentially as shown. The shape coefficient matrix for each branch, all referred to a common origin, is given with a superscript for identification. One of the customary methods of treating a statically indeterminate system is to imagine cuts in the system with the points of cut loaded with equal and opposite redundant forces to maintain continuity. Figure 5A.7 illustrates the cut system. It may be noted that the given system requires a solution to three sets of redundant forces (including moments), and the forces are such that the equilibrium condition is satisfied everywhere.

For each set of redundant forces, a set of elasticity equations can be written, using the proper combination of shape coefficient matrices along the path of action. Where several forces interact, Maxwell's law of reciprocity can be used in writing the equation. The following table summarizes the procedure by which the proper simultaneous equations may be obtained.

![Figure 5A.7](figures/MWK_1956_p0371_fig01_figure-5a-7.png)

> **Table - Summation of Shape Coefficient Matrices For Redundant Forces by Path and Displacements \(EI\)** - see [source crop](tables/MWK_1956_p0371_tbl01_summation-of-shape-coefficient-matrices.png) and needs_extraction

| Redundant Forces | Path | $\bar{F}^2$ | $\bar{F}^4$ | $\bar{F}^4 + \bar{F}^5$ | $\bar{F}^6$ | $\bar{F}^6 + \bar{F}^7 + \bar{F}^8$ | Displacements (EI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\bar{F}^2$ | 0'123 | $A^1 + A^2 + A^3$ | $A^1$ | 0 | $A^1 + A^3$ | 0 | $\delta^3$ |
| $\bar{F}^4$ | 0'14 | $A^1$ | $A^1 + A^4$ | 0 | $A^1$ | 0 | $\delta^5$ |
| $\bar{F}^4 + \bar{F}^5$ | 36 | 0 | 0 | $A^5$ | 0 | 0 | $\delta^5 - \delta^3$ |
| $\bar{F}^6$ | 0'125 | $A^1 + A^3$ | $A^1$ | 0 | $A^1 + A^3 + A^6$ | 0 | $\delta^6$ |
| $\bar{F}^6 + \bar{F}^7 + \bar{F}^8$ | 57 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | $A^7$ | $\delta^7 - \delta^6$ |

Combining the equations and simplifying, the following matrix equation results:

$$EI \begin{vmatrix} \alpha^3 \\ \alpha^5 \\ \alpha^7 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^1 + A^2 + A^3 + A^6 + A^7 & A^1 + A^6 + A^7 & A^1 + A^7 \\ A^1 + A^6 + A^7 & A^1 + A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & A^1 + A^7 \\ A^1 + A^6 + A^7 & A^1 + A^7 & A^1 + A^6 + A^5 + A^7 \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^2 \\ \bar{F}^4 \\ \bar{F}^6 \end{vmatrix} \quad (5A.31)$$

Equation 5A.31 points up the fact that the assembly of shape coefficient matrices along any path of action of the redundant forces can be made automatic by various coding techniques on computers. It is also clear that the final solution requires no specification on how the system is imagined cut.

Suppose in Figure 5A.7, points 3, 4 and 5 were anchors, and members 46 and 67 not existing, we would get a multiple anchor problem. Equation 5A.31 would still be valid except that $A^6$ would vanish and the elements in the displacement column matrix should be $\delta^3$, $\delta^4$ and $\delta^5$.

### 2. Systems with Intermediate Restraints.

Figure 5A.8 shows the same two-anchor and two-loop system with an intermediate restraint at point 8, located between branch points 1 and 2. Denote the shape coefficient matrix for branch 18 as $A^8$. Then the following matrix equation can be written:

---

A MATRIX METHOD OF PIPING ANALYSIS AND USE OF DIGITAL COMPUTERS 371

$$EI \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}^{1} \\ \bar{a}^{2} \\ \bar{a}^{3} \\ \bar{a}^{8} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{8} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} \\ A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{6} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} \\ A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} \\ A^{1} & A^{1} & A^{1} & A^{1} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^{8} \\ \bar{F}^{6} \\ \bar{F}^{4} \\ \bar{F}^{P_8} \end{vmatrix}$$

(5A.32)

![Figure 5A.8](figures/MWK_1956_p0372_fig01_figure-5a-8.png)

So far, all the forces and displacements are referred to the common origin. To account for the effects of stops occurring at point 8, it is necessary to modify Eq. 5A.32. Let $\bar{F}^{88}$ be the force (including moment) vector at point 8, but not referred to the origin; and $\bar{a}^{88}$ be the corresponding displacement (including rotation) vector at point 8 with respect to the undeformed position of point 8. We have:

$$\bar{F}^{8} = K_{08} \bar{F}^{88},$$
$$\bar{a}^{88} = K'_{80} \bar{a}^{8},$$

(5A.33)

where,

$$K_{08} = \begin{vmatrix} I & \begin{matrix} 0 & -q_{3} & q_{2} \\ q_{3} & 0 & -q_{1} \\ -q_{2} & q_{1} & 0 \end{matrix} \\ O & I \end{vmatrix}$$

(5A.34)

$$K'_{80} = \begin{vmatrix} I & O \\ \begin{matrix} 0 & -q_{3} & q_{2} \\ q_{3} & 0 & -q_{1} \\ -q_{2} & q_{1} & 0 \end{matrix} & I \end{vmatrix}$$

and $q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}$ are the coordinates of point 8. Upon substitution of Eq. 5A.33, Eq. 5A.32 becomes:

$$EI \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}^{1} \\ \bar{a}^{2} \\ \bar{a}^{3} \\ \bar{a}^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{8} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{6} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{P_8} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^{8} \\ \bar{F}^{6} \\ \bar{F}^{4} \\ \bar{F}^{88} \end{vmatrix}$$

Since from Eq. 5A.34, $K_{08} K'_{80} = I$, the last equation may be modified as follows:

$$EI \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}^{1} \\ \bar{a}^{2} \\ \bar{a}^{3} \\ \bar{a}^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{8} + A^{P_8} & A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{8} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{6} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} K_{08} \\ A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{7} & A^{1} + A^{2} + A^{P_8} & (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \\ K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} A^{1} & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) & K'_{80} (A^{1} + A^{8}) K_{08} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{F}^{8} \\ \bar{F}^{6} \\ \bar{F}^{4} \\ \bar{F}^{88} \end{vmatrix}$$

(5A.35)

Equation 5A.35 is applicable to cases having orthogonal rigid stops whose directions coincide with the directions of the chosen coordinate axes. For orthogonal elastic stops, we must include the effects of elastic

---

$$
EI \begin{vmatrix} \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \alpha^{88} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^1 + A^2 + A^4 + A^5 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & (A^2 + A^4)K_{15} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^3 + A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4K_{56} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & (A^4 + A^6)K_{56} \\ K'_{15}(A^2 + A^4) & K'_{56}A^4 & K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6) & K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6)K_{56} + A^x \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} F^a \\ F^a \\ F^a \\ F^{aa} \end{vmatrix}
$$

(5A.36)

where $A^* = \text{diag.} \, [1/x_1, 1/x_2, 1/x_3, 1/x_4, 1/x_5, 1/x_6]$, and $x_p$ ($p = 1, \ldots, 6$) are spring constants of moments and forces for the orthogonal elastic stops.

In the case of a skew force-stop which has direction cosines with the fixed coordinate axes as $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$, Eq. 5A.36 will be modified to be:

$$
EI \begin{vmatrix} \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \delta^7 \\ \alpha_{\text{skew}} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} A^1 + A^2 + A^4 + A^5 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & (A^2 + A^4)K_{15}\overline{\beta} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^3 + A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4K_{56}\overline{\beta} \\ A^2 + A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^7 & A^4 + A^6 + A^7 & (A^4 + A^6)K_{56}\overline{\beta} \\ \overline{\beta}^T K'_{15}A^4 & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}A^4 & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6) & \overline{\beta}^T K'_{56}(A^4 + A^6)K_{56} + A^x\overline{\beta} \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} F^a \\ F^a \\ F^a \\ F_{\text{skew}} \end{vmatrix}
$$

(5A.37)

where $F_{\text{skew}}$ is the skew force and $\alpha_{\text{skew}}$ the skew displacement. They bear the following relationships with $\overline{F}^{88}$ and $\alpha^{88}$:

$$
F_{\text{skew}} = \overline{F}^{88}, \quad (5A.38)
$$
$$
\alpha_{\text{skew}} = \overline{\beta}^T \alpha^{88},
$$

where

$$
\overline{\beta}^T = [0, 0, 0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3]. \quad (5A.39)
$$

## 5A-4 An Example

Figure 5A.9 shows a sketch of a reactor coolant loop representing a piping system with two anchors, one closed loop, and four elastic stops. Thus, a total of sixteen unknown moments and forces has to be determined.

Page 375 shows the input to the machine. By using the table marked "Key to Input Data", the input is self-explanatory. It should be noted that the flexibility factor (k) and the stress intensification factor (i) for curved members are automatically calculated if not specified.

Page 375 also shows the check of coordinates of the end points of each branch.

Page 376 (at top) shows the restraining moments and forces on anchors and stops as well as on additional points specified on the SUM-line on the input sheet A. The total actions on the anchor at the reactor are obtained by adding those for points 1 and 101. The maximum stress in the system is also automatically recorded.

Page 376 also gives the stresses, moments, deflections and rotations at each point of the system. Since a curved member in the input is denoted by a radius only, the machine calculates the tangent points which are indicated as A and B.

Finally page 377 gives the moments, forces and coordinates referred to the origin at the anchors, stops and intersections. These moments and forces are actually those from the solution of the equations. A complete print-out of the equations and the inversion of the same may be obtained by substituting an IND-card for an END-card. Utilizing this device, it is possible to split a complicated piping system into two or more parts if the capacity of the machine is insufficient to solve the required number of equations.

## 5A-5 Selected Bibliography

Since 1956, considerable literature has been published, using matrix algebra. Brock's comprehensive treatment\* of the piping problem, using matrix methods, stimulated wide interests in this method. The author treated first the two-anchor problem subject to expansion, then the problem of two anchors with restraints and finally, the multiple-anchor problem with restraints. The shape coefficient matrices for straight members as well as circular bends situated in one of the principal coordinate planes, and a straight member skewed in space were given. Soule (1) † introduced "the connecting tensor," which enables one to solve, with greater facility, a problem with multiple branch intersection points. This scheme was extended subsequently to the closed loop problem by the same author (4). Peck et al. (5) reiterated Brock's transfer matrix for shape coefficients, and generalized it to solve loop problems by synthesizing the piping system so that the size of matrices is no larger than 6 × 6, the procedure being similar to the well-known inversion method. In the same paper, a method was also suggested for obtaining shape coefficients for any pipe through integration, the integrand being the product of five matrices. Chen (6) proposed a method by which a multiple anchor and loop problem can be handled in a systematic manner. The summing of stiffness (the inverse of flexibility) matrices of various interconnecting members follows a logical pattern consistent with the piping configuration. The effects of uniform and concentrated loads on straight, planar members were treated by Soule (2). A general, mathematical solution for weight effects on straight and curved members was proposed by Owens (7), and later illustrated (8) by its application to a planar structure with straight members. Inspired by Brock's matrix approach, Crawford (3) elaborated on the effect of concentrated loads and extended the method to dynamic loadings.

Many other pertinent publications have not been reviewed here due to space limitations. The reviewed ones are listed below in the order of the date of publication.

1. J. W. Soule, "The Solution of Multiple-Branch Piping Flexibility Problems by Tensor Analysis," Jl. of App. Mech., Trans. ASME, Vol. 78, 1956, pp. 176–180.
2. J. W. Soule, "Tensor-Flexibility Analysis of Pipe-Supporting Systems," Ibid., pp. 181–184.
3. L. Crawford, "Pipe Stress Analysis for Static and Dynamic Loading," Trans. Soc. of Naval Arch. and Marine Engrs., Vol. 65, 1957, p. 197.
4. J. W. Soule, "Tensor Flexibility Analysis of Closed-Loop Piping Systems," Jl. of App. Mech., Trans. ASME, Vol. 80, 1958, pp. 11–16.
5. L. G. Peck, R. F. Meyer, F. F. Strong and H. Kalsen, "The Automatic Calculation of Forces and Deflections in Piping Systems," Trans. ASME, Vol. 80, 1958, pp. 235–244.
6. L. H. Chen, "Piping Flexibility Analysis by Stiffness Matrix," Jl. of Appl. Mech., Trans. ASME, Vol. 81, 1959, pp. 608–612.
7. R. H. Owens, "Flexibility Analysis of Piping Systems Formulated for Digital Computer Solution," Proc. 3rd U. S. Nat. Cong. of App. Mech., pp. 419–430.
8. R. H. Owens, "An Elementary Development of Piping Flexibility Analysis with Illustrative Example," A.S.N.E. Jl., Feb. 1960.

\* "Design of Piping Systems," see Appendix A, Section A-2, "Bibliography on Piping Flexibility and Stress Analysis," pp. 297–299, reference '96/.

† Number in brackets refers to the Selected Bibliography of this Chapter.
